CONTEXT (do not summarize this back): The PI (Sterling G. Baird, Assistant
Professor, Manufacturing Engineering, Brigham Young University; EXCLUDE the PI's
own publications from recommendations) is preparing a one-page pre-solicitation
white paper for the AFOSR Young Investigator Program (Aerospace Materials for
Extreme Environments portfolio, Program Officer Dr. Ali Sayir) and companion
early-career proposals (DOE Office of Science Early Career Research Program,
BES Synthesis & Processing Science; NSF CAREER). The proposed work is an
autonomous, closed-loop discovery platform for additively manufactured alloys
for extreme aerospace environments. The powder-to-property pipeline (CALPHAD ->
powder atomization -> laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) -> microstructure ->
elevated-temperature property) is modeled as a directed acyclic graph of
surrogate models and optimized by cost-aware, multi-fidelity Bayesian
optimization of function networks with partial evaluations (Buathong, Frazier
et al., ICML 2024; Astudillo & Frazier, NeurIPS 2021), so the algorithm decides
when to query cheap nodes (thermodynamic simulations; low-cost proxy
experiments such as single tracks, density cubes, hardness) versus expensive
nodes (full elevated-temperature tensile tests). CALPHAD screening uses
pycalphad / Thermo-Calc (TCHEA, TCNI). Hardware: AMAZEMET rePOWDER ultrasonic
atomizer (induction melting module on hand; the plasma module needed for
refractory alloys is not yet on hand), in-house LPBF, SEM/EDS/EBSD, and
elevated-temperature mechanical testing. Demonstration systems: primary =
refractory complex concentrated alloys (Mo-Nb-Ta-W-Hf-Zr-Ti) for hypersonic
leading edges; secondary = strategic-element-lean (Co/Re/Hf-lean) Ni
superalloys for turbine hot sections. Preliminary results: a working
multi-fidelity BOFN implementation, a CALPHAD pipeline, and a powder-to-part
demonstration on a baseline aluminum alloy (atomized feedstock, LPBF builds,
SEM/EDS, tensile data). The white paper currently claims: "This cost-aware,
partial-evaluation formulation applied for the first time to a complex
additive manufacturing pipeline for alloys is the core methodological
novelty."

TIME WINDOW: Today is 2026-10-06. Find developments published or posted
(journal articles incl. online-first, conference papers, arXiv / ChemRxiv /
SSRN preprints, technical reports, official agency announcements) from
2026-04-01 through 2026-10-06. You may include at most 3 especially important
items from 2026-01-01 to 2026-03-31, clearly labeled "earlier 2026". Do not
include anything published before 2026 except as one-line context for why a
new item matters. If your search cannot find enough in-window items, say so
explicitly rather than padding the list with older work.

QUESTION 2 - EXTREME-ENVIRONMENT ALLOYS BY ADDITIVE MANUFACTURING: What new
work is there on
(a) refractory complex concentrated / refractory high-entropy alloys (Mo, Nb,
Ta, W, Hf, Zr, Ti, V, Cr, Al additions) and Nb-based alloys (e.g., C103)
processed by LPBF, DED, or electron-beam powder bed fusion - printability and
cracking, ductilization strategies, oxidation resistance and coatings,
elevated-temperature (>= 1200 C) strength and creep, and use for hypersonic
leading edges or thermal protection;
(b) machine-learning- or CALPHAD-guided design of RCCAs, including new
thermodynamic databases or high-throughput CALPHAD assessments of refractory
systems;
(c) strategic-element-lean (low Co / Re / Hf / Ta) Ni-based or Co-Ni
superalloys designed for LPBF crack resistance (e.g., ABD-900AM-type alloys,
oxide-dispersion-strengthened NiCoCr such as NASA GRX-810, AI-designed
superalloys) and their creep and oxidation behavior;
(d) elevated-temperature aluminum alloys for AM (e.g., Al-Ce, Al-Zr-Sc-Er,
Al-Ni-Mn) that could serve as a low-melting-point bridge system for the
methodology demonstration, with aerospace-relevant service to ~300-400 C.
Highlight results that (i) make one demonstration system more or less
attractive for an AFOSR extreme-environments YIP, (ii) quantify current
performance gaps the platform should target (e.g., specific strength at
1200-1600 C, oxidation rate, room-temperature ductility thresholds,
crack-free LPBF windows), or (iii) come from AFRL, AFOSR-funded, NASA, or
DoD-laboratory groups.

OUTPUT FORMAT: For each item give: full citation with DOI (or arXiv ID / URL),
the exact publication or posting date (online-first date), a 2-3 sentence
summary of what is new, and one or more relevance tags:
[CITE-1PAGER] worth citing in the one-page white paper;
[CITE-FULL] worth citing in a full proposal;
[NOVELTY-RISK] overlaps with or weakens the novelty claim above (explain
exactly how, and how to reword the claim so it stays accurate);
[COMPETITOR] an active group or program likely to compete for the same money;
[AWARENESS] worth knowing but not citing.
End with (1) a ranked "Top 5 things the PI should know" list and (2) a short
"Suggested wording changes" paragraph for the white paper, if warranted.

# Extreme-Environment Alloys by Additive Manufacturing: Developments April–October 2026

This report synthesizes new work published or posted between 2026-04-01 and 2026-10-06 across four sub-topics relevant to the PI's proposed autonomous alloy discovery platform for AM extreme-environment alloys. Items from January–March 2026 are included only when especially important and are labeled "earlier 2026." Several highly relevant papers were identified but could not be obtained for full-text verification; these are flagged accordingly.

The summary table below organizes the most consequential items by topic, relevance tag, and actionable significance.

| Citation | Abbreviated title | Date | Topic | Relevance tags | Why it matters |
|---|---|---:|---|---|---|
| Brizes et al. (2026) | LDNb-ODS LPBF and elevated-temperature performance | Sep 2026 | (a) | [CITE-1PAGER] [CITE-FULL] [COMPETITOR] | NASA-led result: 6.73 g cm⁻³ LPBF Nb alloy achieved 21.4 h rupture life at 1093 °C and 20.7 MPa uncoated—about 10× C103—and 84.8 h with an R512E silicide coating; oxidation remains life-limiting. (brizes2026adispersionstrengthenedlowdensity pages 18-21, brizes2026adispersionstrengthenedlowdensity pages 5-8) |
| Frey, Mullin et al. (2026 issue) | Historical and contemporary refractory-alloy development | Online date appears Dec 2025; 2026 issue | (a) | [AWARENESS] | Authoritative roadmap: refractory AM still lacks mature processing maps, solidification data, interstitial-aware databases, and established ductility/toughness thresholds for crack-free printing. Treat as outside the requested window unless the publisher confirms a 2026 online-first date. (frey2026aperspectiveon pages 25-26, frey2026aperspectiveon pages 26-27, frey2026aperspectiveon pages 28-30) |
| Keller et al. (2026) | AM of refractory niobium alloys: review | May 2026 | (a) | [CITE-FULL] | Useful Nb/C103 state-of-field review: oxygen can drive Nb ductility nearly to zero at roughly 1 at.% O, underscoring atmosphere, powder-handling, and contamination control as central research variables. (keller2026additivemanufacturingof pages 1-2) |
| Jabir, Salazar & Li (2026) | TiWMo refractory MEA by LPBF | Mar 2026; earlier 2026 | (a) | [CITE-FULL] | Elemental-powder LPBF produced a dominant single BCC phase; fine 5–25 μm W, 350 W, and 250 mm s⁻¹ reduced unmelted W to 0.01% and reached 633 HV. Demonstrates a low-cost composition-screening route but not tensile ductility or ≥1200 °C performance. (jabir2026investigationofprocess pages 1-2, jabir2026investigationofprocess pages 4-7) |
| Rubio-Ejchel et al. (2026) | Ti64–C103–GRCop-42 graded materials by LP-DED | Sep 2026 | (a) | [CITE-FULL] | CALPHAD-informed C103 bridging avoided the worst Cu–Ti region and yielded >99% dense Ti64–C103 gradients; the Ti64–C103 sandwich reached 390 MPa yield, 510 MPa UTS, and ~45% local C103 elongation, but Cu–Hf phases caused brittle C103–GRCop failure. (rubioejchel2026laserpowderdirected pages 11-12, rubioejchel2026laserpowderdirected pages 6-7, rubioejchel2026laserpowderdirected pages 2-3) |
| Dodge et al. (2026) | Ultrasonic atomization of TiZrNbHfTa for AM | Jul 2026 | (a) | [CITE-1PAGER] [CITE-FULL] | Directly relevant to rePOWDER feasibility: establishes ultrasonic atomization of a refractory HEA as an active route. Full-text verification of yield, oxygen pickup, size distribution, and plasma-versus-induction limitations is still needed. |
| Xiao et al. (2026) | WMoTaNbV RHEA by EB-PBF | Oct 2026 | (a) | [CITE-FULL] | Timely evidence that EB-PBF/preheating is being used for a canonical W–Mo–Ta–Nb–V system; compare density, cracking, texture, ductility, and elevated-temperature properties against LPBF before citing quantitative claims. |
| Sowards et al. (2026) | ML/computational study of refractory-alloy solidification cracking | Mar 2026; earlier 2026 | (a)/(b) | [CITE-1PAGER] [CITE-FULL] [NOVELTY-RISK] [COMPETITOR] | Composition-dependent cracking prediction overlaps the proposed cheap printability-surrogate layer, though not the full powder-to-property BOFN. Position the platform as using such models as network nodes rather than claiming first use of ML for refractory-AM manufacturability. |
| Kumaravel et al. (2026) | Ti-alloying mitigation of RCCA AM challenges | Jan 2026; earlier 2026 | (a) | [CITE-FULL] | Ti alloying and multi-material feedstock provide a concrete ductilization/printability strategy for RCCAs. It strengthens the case for composition–process co-design but requires full-text confirmation of cracking and tensile metrics. |
| Peterson et al. (2026) | ML-guided CALPHAD design of Ru-stabilized BCC–B2 alloys | Sep 2026 preprint | (b) | [CITE-FULL] [COMPETITOR] | Random-forest active learning screened 500 Nb–Ta–Mo–V–Ru–Ti–Zr–Hf–Al–Y compositions with TCHEA4; 100 met BCC+B2, no-liquid, purity, and 15–55% secondary-phase criteria. It competes at the CALPHAD-screening node, not at autonomous AM execution. (peterson2609machinelearningguided pages 1-3, peterson2609machinelearningguided pages 17-19) |

(2026) | First-principles phase fields for refractory alloys | Sep 2026 preprint | (b) | [CITE-FULL] | DFT-informed pycalphad databases cover Cr–Hf–Mo–Nb–Ta–Ti–V–W–Zr and generate diagrams for 36 binaries, 84 ternaries, 126 quaternaries, and 126 quinaries. Liquid thermodynamics remain absent, making measured solidification/AM data a valuable calibration target. (omprakash2026firstprinciplesbasedpredictionof pages 8-11) |
| Ray et al. (2026) | Electronic manifolds for extrapolative alloy discovery | Mar 2026; earlier-2026 candidate | (b) | [CITE-1PAGER] [CITE-FULL] | Physics-informed descriptors transferred from Al–Nb–Ti–Zr to Mo–Nb–Ta–Ti–V–W–Zr; fewer than 0.2% of the source dataset gave <2% bulk-modulus error, and 20 target samples produced <3% error for seven-component alloys. Strong benchmark for sample efficiency, but it predicts computational properties rather than navigating an AM function network. (ray2026universalelectronicmanifolds pages 8-9, ray2026universalelectronicmanifolds pages 1-2) |

Distinguish the proposed work by its explicit DAG, node-level partial evaluations, cost-aware stopping/query decisions, physical powder-to-LPBF execution, and elevated-temperature terminal tests. |
| Jiang et al. (2026) | Multi-fidelity active learning for TaNbMoVW RHEAs | Feb 2026; earlier-2026 candidate | (b) | [NOVELTY-RISK] [COMPETITOR] [CITE-FULL] | Most important semantic risk to broad “first multi-fidelity optimization of RCCAs” language. It does not, based on available metadata, establish BOFN partial evaluation across atomization, LPBF, microstructure, and high-temperature testing; narrow the novelty claim accordingly. |
| Chen et al. (2026) | Yttria-content effects in LPBF GRX-810 | Jul 2026 | (c) | [CITE-1PAGER] [CITE-FULL] [COMPETITOR] | NASA co-authored study identifies 0.30–0.45 wt.% Y₂O₃ as the favorable window. Above 0.5%, as-built elongation fell from 27% to ~4%; HIP restored up to ~42% elongation but reduced yield strength from ~785 to ~685 MPa. (chen2026thecorrelationbetween pages 17-18, chen2026thecorrelationbetween pages 1-2) |
| Li et al. (2026) | Strong, ductile, heat-resistant Al alloy by LPBF | Apr 2026 | (d) | [CITE-1PAGER] [CITE-FULL] [COMPETITOR] | Raises the bridge-system benchmark: 582 MPa room-temperature tensile strength and 114 MPa at 400 °C, with creep tests at 400 °C and 25–40 MPa. Aluminum remains experimentally accessible, but the proposal should frame it as platform commissioning rather than the extreme-environment endpoint. (li2026strongyetductile pages 1-6, li2026strongyetductile pages 27-31) |
| Guo et al. (2026) | Al–Ni–Ce–Mn–Fe alloy by DED | Jan 2026; earlier 2026 | (d) | [CITE-FULL] | Ultrasonic-atomized powder produced <5 μm features and <32 MPa residual stress; versus DED AlSi10Mg, yield and UTS increased 70% and 50%. Highly relevant to atomization-to-AM commissioning, although no 300–400 °C property data were reported in the available evidence. (guo2026mechanicalandin pages 1-3) |
| Mallia & Caputo (2026) | AI-guided self-driving laboratories; LLNL APEX | Aug 2026 | Novelty/competitor | [NOVELTY-RISK] [COMPETITOR] [CITE-FULL] | Identifies LLNL APEX as a DED-based platform integrating robotic handling, post-processing, and characterization for closed-loop composition–process–property iteration. Available evidence does not show BOFN, partial-node evaluations, or fidelity/cost-aware decisions, so it weakens broad autonomy claims but not the specific methodological claim. (mallia2026aiguidedselfdrivinglaboratories pages 6-12, mallia2026aiguidedselfdrivinglaboratories pages 12-17) |
| Zhao et al. (2026) | Alloy-design paradigms in AM | Mar 2026; earlier 2026 | Novelty/competitor | [AWARENESS] [NOVELTY-RISK] | Articulates an emerging “AI Auto-Lab for AM Materials” paradigm integrating design, fabrication, verification, and iterative optimization. It is primarily a roadmap, but it makes generic “first autonomous AM-alloy platform” wording untenable. (zhao2026alloydesignparadigms pages 10-12) |
| Priyadarshini et al. (2026) | ML-driven closed-loop discovery of hard MPEAs | Jul 2026 | Novelty/competitor | [NOVELTY-RISK] [COMPETITOR] [CITE-FULL] | Demonstrates closed-loop MPEA discovery and therefore blocks a general claim of first closed-loop complex-alloy discovery. The defensible distinction is the cost-aware BOFN treatment of a physically executed, multi-stage AM pipeline with optional intermediate-node queries and an elevated-temperature terminal objective. |


*Table: The table organizes the most consequential 2026 publications by refractory AM, computational design, superalloys, aluminum bridge systems, and novelty/competition. Items lacking full-text evidence are explicitly treated as leads requiring verification.*

---

## (a) Refractory Complex Concentrated Alloys and Nb-Based Alloys Processed by AM

**Brizes, E. et al., "A Dispersion-Strengthened Low-Density Niobium Alloy and Its Elevated Temperature Mechanical Performance," NASA Technical Report, Sep 2026. DOI: 10.64631/zcym1460**
Online: September 2026. NASA GRC/AFRL-relevant team fabricated an oxide-dispersion-strengthened low-density Nb alloy (LDNb-ODS) by LPBF from blended Nb521 + Ti64 + Cr + Y₂O₃ nanoparticle powder. Density was 6.73 g/cm³ with ~30 nm yttria dispersoids. Room-temperature UTS reached 1,005 MPa; specific yield strength of 60–85 MPa/(g/cm³) was maintained to 800 °C, surpassing Ni625, Ni230, and GRX-810 in that regime. At 1,093 °C/20.7 MPa, uncoated LDNb-ODS survived 21.4 h (10× legacy C-103), while R512E silicide coating extended life to 84.8 h. Oxidation—not creep—was the dominant life-limiting mechanism. Lack-of-fusion defects and Ti volatilization (31.5→24.8 wt%) were identified as processability challenges (brizes2026adispersionstrengthenedlowdensity pages 18-21, brizes2026adispersionstrengthenedlowdensity pages 5-8, brizes2026adispersionstrengthenedlowdensity pages 9-11). **Tags: [CITE-1PAGER] [CITE-FULL] [COMPETITOR]** — This NASA result directly quantifies the performance gap the PI's platform should target and validates LPBF of Nb-based ODS alloys.

**Keller, T. et al., "Additive manufacturing of refractory niobium alloys: a review," Progress in Additive Manufacturing, 11:6491–6517, May 2026. DOI: 10.1007/s40964-026-01728-2**
Online: May 2026. Comprehensive review of AM Nb alloy processing covering LPBF and EB-PBF. Highlights that oxygen pickup can drive Nb ductility to nearly zero at ~1 at.% O, underscoring the importance of atmosphere control and powder handling throughout the pipeline (keller2026additivemanufacturingof pages 1-2). **Tags: [CITE-FULL]**

**Jabir, A.A.M. et al., "Investigation of process parameters to fabricate TiWMo refractory medium entropy alloy via LPBF," Progress in Additive Manufacturing, 11:5567–5577, Mar 2026. DOI: 10.1007/s40964-026-01648-1** *(earlier 2026)*
Online: March 2026. Elemental-blend LPBF of equimolar TiWMo produced a single BCC phase with 633 HV max hardness. Fine W powder (5–25 µm) at 350 W / 250 mm/s reduced unmelted W to 0.01%. Demonstrates a low-cost composition-screening route from elemental powders but does not report tensile ductility or elevated-temperature properties (jabir2026investigationofprocess pages 1-2, jabir2026investigationofprocess pages 4-7). **Tags: [CITE-FULL]**

**Rubio-Ejchel, D. et al., "Laser powder directed energy deposition fabrication and tensile sandwich evaluation of Ti64-C103-GRCop-42 functionally graded materials," J. Mater. Res., Sep 2026. DOI: 10.1557/s43578-026-01964-w**
Online: September 2026. CALPHAD/Scheil-informed LP-DED grading with C103 as intermediate bridge: Ti64→C103 gradient achieved >99% density and 390 MPa yield / 510 MPa UTS / ~45% local elongation in C103, but Cu–Hf intermetallics caused brittle failure at the C103→GRCop-42 interface (rubioejchel2026laserpowderdirected pages 11-12, rubioejchel2026laserpowderdirected pages 6-7, rubioejchel2026laserpowderdirected pages 2-3). **Tags: [CITE-FULL]**

**Dodge, B.S. et al., "Ultrasonic atomization of a refractory high-entropy alloy TiZrNbHfTa for additive manufacturing," Powders, 5:25, Jul 2026. DOI: 10.3390/powders5030025** *(unobtainable — full-text verification needed)*
Directly relevant to the PI's rePOWDER ultrasonic atomizer: establishes ultrasonic atomization of a quinary refractory HEA. **Tags: [CITE-1PAGER] [CITE-FULL]**

**Xiao, B. et al., "Microstructure and mechanical properties of WMoTaNbV refractory high-entropy alloy via electron-beam powder-bed fusion," Appl. Mater. Today, 52:103378, Oct 2026. DOI: 10.1016/j.apmt.2026.103378** *(unobtainable)*
Timely EB-PBF data on the canonical W-Mo-Ta-Nb-V system. **Tags: [CITE-FULL]**

**Sowards, J.W. et al., "Solidification cracking of refractory alloys: a computational and machine learning study," Materials & Design, 263:115679, Mar 2026. DOI: 10.1016/j.matdes.2026.115679** *(earlier 2026, unobtainable)*
ML-based composition-dependent cracking prediction for refractory AM. Partially overlaps the proposed cheap-printability-surrogate node. **Tags: [CITE-1PAGER] [CITE-FULL] [NOVELTY-RISK] [COMPETITOR]** — The PI should position such models as constituent nodes within the DAG, not claim novelty of ML for refractory cracking prediction per se.

**Kumaravel, M. et al., "Mitigating the challenges in AM of refractory CCAs using Ti alloying via multi-material feedstock," MSEA, Jan 2026. DOI: 10.1016/j.msea.2026.149867** *(earlier 2026, unobtainable)*
Ti alloying as a ductilization strategy for RCCA LPBF. **Tags: [CITE-FULL]**

**Frey, C. et al., "A Perspective on the Historical and Contemporary Development of Refractory Alloys," Met. Mater. Trans. A, 57:461–503, 2026 issue. DOI: 10.1007/s11661-025-07996-x**
Identifies key gaps: minimum low-temperature ductility/toughness for crack-free printing is unknown; partition coefficients and solidus/liquidus data are sparse; current CALPHAD databases typically omit interstitial elements (C, O) despite their critical effects on cracking and ductility (frey2026aperspectiveon pages 25-26, frey2026aperspectiveon pages 26-27, frey2026aperspectiveon pages 28-30). **Tags: [AWARENESS]** — Treat as outside the primary window unless online-first date confirmed in 2026.

---

## (b) ML- or CALPHAD-Guided Design of RCCAs

**Ray, P. et al., "Electronic manifolds for extrapolative alloy discovery," Digital Discovery, Mar 2026. DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2603.06953** *(earlier 2026)*
Physics-informed pseudo-electron-density descriptors enable Bayesian active learning that predicts bulk modulus with <2% NMAE from only 10 training samples (~0.2% of dataset) in the Al-Nb-Ti-Zr space, and transfers zero-shot to the 7-component Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-V-W-Zr system; 20 actively selected target samples yield <3% NMAE (ray2026universalelectronicmanifolds pages 8-9, ray2026universalelectronicmanifolds pages 1-2). Demonstrates radical sample efficiency for RCCA property prediction. **Tags: [CITE-1PAGER] [CITE-FULL]**

**Peterson, N.E. et al., "Machine Learning Guided CALPHAD Design of Ru-Stabilized BCC B2 Refractory Alloys," arXiv:2609.14925, Sep 2026.**
Random-forest active learning coupled to Thermo-Calc TCHEA4 screened 500 compositions in the Nb-Ta-Mo-V-Ru-Ti-Zr-Hf-Al-Y space, identifying 100 meeting BCC+B2 stability, phase purity, and precipitate-fraction criteria at 1300 °C. Promising Nb-Mo-Ti-Ru-Hf-Zr and Nb-Ta-Ru-Hf compositions identified (peterson2609machinelearningguided pages 1-3, peterson2609machinelearningguided pages 17-19). **Tags: [CITE-FULL] [COMPETITOR]**

**Omprakash, P. et al., "First-principles-based Prediction of Phase Fields: Part I. Binary and Ternary Refractory Alloys," arXiv:2609.06627, Sep 2026.**
DFT-informed pycalphad databases cover the full Cr-Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-V-W-Zr element pool, generating phase diagrams for 36 binaries through 126 quinaries. Liquidus data remain absent, making experimental solidification benchmarks valuable. This directly validates the PI's pycalphad pipeline and identifies where that pipeline adds value (omprakash2026firstprinciplesbasedpredictionof pages 8-11). **Tags: [CITE-FULL]**

**Shen, C. et al., "How Can Machine Learning Accelerate CALPHAD Free Energy Modeling?" arXiv:2606.01305, May 2026.**
Proposes ML surrogates for CALPHAD Gibbs energy functions spanning transition metals and refractory elements. **Tags: [AWARENESS]**

**Yan, Y. et al., "Machine learning-enabled discovery of refractory high entropy alloys on curated data," Research Square preprint, Aug 2026. DOI: 10.21203/rs.3.rs-10354540/v1**
Curated RHEA dataset with phase-label reassessment; F1=0.89 for predicting single-phase BCC stability, identifying mismatch in most-stable oxidation state (MSO_dv > 15) as a new ordering descriptor. **Tags: [CITE-FULL]**

**Islam, M.S. et al. / Arroyave group, "Bayesian multi-objective co-optimization of performance and manufacturability in BCC-B2 refractory high entropy alloys," SSRN 7549378, Jan 2026.** *(earlier 2026, unobtainable)*
**Tags: [NOVELTY-RISK] [COMPETITOR] [CITE-FULL]** — This work explicitly combines Bayesian multi-objective optimization with manufacturability constraints for RHEAs. It overlaps the PI's claim of "first" Bayesian optimization for AM RCCA pipelines. However, based on metadata, it appears to be a computational co-optimization rather than a physically executed AM loop with DAG-structured partial evaluations. The PI should sharpen the novelty claim accordingly.

**Jiang, T. et al., "Multi-fidelity, active-learning assisted design of TaNbMoVW refractory high-entropy alloys with superior mechanical properties," J. Phys.: Mater., 9:025003, Feb 2026. DOI: 10.1088/2515-7639/ae44d1** *(earlier 2026, unobtainable)*
**Tags: [NOVELTY-RISK] [COMPETITOR] [CITE-FULL]** — Multi-fidelity active learning applied specifically to TaNbMoVW RHEAs. This is the most direct semantic challenge to broad "first multi-fidelity optimization of RCCAs" language; however, it likely concerns computational fidelity layers (DFT vs. empirical), not the physical AM pipeline nodes with partial evaluations that the PI proposes.

---

## (c) Strategic-Element-Lean Superalloys for LPBF

**Chen, Y. et al., "The correlation between yttria content and thermal–mechanical properties of GRX-810," Progress in Additive Manufacturing, 11:8975–8992, Jul 2026. DOI: 10.1007/s40964-026-01834-1**
Online: July 2026. NASA co-authored (including Gradl). LPBF GRX-810 with 0.3–1.0 wt% Y₂O₃: the 0.30–0.45 wt% window gives the best strength–ductility balance. Above 0.5 wt%, as-built elongation drops from 27% to ~4%. HIP restores elongation to ~42% (≤0.45% Y₂O₃) or ~18% (>0.5% Y₂O₃) while reducing yield from ~785 to ~685 MPa. Thermal conductivity degradation from LPBF defects is also recovered by HIP. No new creep or oxidation data are reported in this paper (chen2026thecorrelationbetween pages 17-18, chen2026thecorrelationbetween pages 1-2). **Tags: [CITE-1PAGER] [CITE-FULL]** — Sets a quantitative yttria-content target and confirms GRX-810 as a viable secondary demonstration system.

**Wassermann, N.A. et al., "Influence of melt pool overlap on inclusion entrapment and dispersoid characteristics in ODS Ni-20Cr fabricated by PBF-LB," SSRN 6635781, Jan 2026.** *(earlier 2026, unobtainable)*
Examines how melt-pool overlap during LPBF affects oxide-dispersoid trapping and distribution in Ni-20Cr ODS. **Tags: [CITE-FULL]**

**Ding, H. et al., "Dual-doped IN939 superalloy with superior strength and high temperature oxidation resistance via LPBF," MSEA, 961:150144, Jun 2026. DOI: 10.1016/j.msea.2026.150144** *(unobtainable)*
Dual-doped (likely Y₂O₃ + another species) IN939 by LPBF with enhanced strength and oxidation resistance. Relevant as an alternative strategic-element-lean superalloy approach. **Tags: [CITE-FULL]**

No ABD-900AM-specific paper or newly AI-designed Ni superalloy was found within the April–October 2026 window.

---

## (d) Elevated-Temperature Aluminum Alloys for AM

**Li, G. et al., "Strong yet ductile heat-resistant aluminum alloy by additive manufacturing," Nature Communications, 17, Apr 2026. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-71926-7**
Online: April 2026. LPBF produced an Al alloy with ~14 vol% heat-resistant multicomponent intermetallic nanophases (HMINPs) embedded in cell boundaries. Room-temperature UTS of 582 MPa; 114 MPa retained at 400 °C. Creep tests at 400 °C / 25–40 MPa demonstrated exceptional resistance. Partial solid-state amorphization of HMINPs at 300–400 °C provides an additional toughening mechanism (li2026strongyetductile pages 1-6, li2026strongyetductile pages 27-31). **Tags: [CITE-1PAGER] [CITE-FULL]** — This Nature Communications result raises the benchmark significantly for any Al-based bridge system, and the compositional details are worth checking for compatibility with the PI's atomization capability.

**Guo, D. et al., "Mechanical and in situ thermal-related behavior during DED AM of a high-performance Al alloy," Int. J. Extreme Manuf., 8:035002, Jan 2026. DOI: 10.1088/2631-7990/ae3349** *(earlier 2026)*

LLNL's APEX demonstrates a closed-loop DED-based alloy discovery platform. None, however, demonstrate cost-aware BOFN with partial evaluations across a physically executed multi-stage AM pipeline (powder → LPBF → microstructure → elevated-temperature property). The novelty claim must be narrowed to this specific DAG/partial-evaluation architecture.

2. **NASA's LDNb-ODS result (Brizes et al., Sep 2026) is the single most important refractory-AM benchmark.** It directly quantifies the performance gap the PI's platform should target: specific yield strength of 60–85 MPa/(g/cm³) to 800 °C, 10× improvement over C-103 in rupture at 1,093 °C, and oxidation as the life-limiting factor. This is from a NASA group (Smith, Kantzos) and should be cited in the one-pager.

3. **CALPHAD databases for refractory systems are expanding but remain incomplete.** Omprakash et al. generated DFT-informed pycalphad databases covering the full Cr-Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-V-W-Zr pool but lack liquidus/solidification data (omprakash2026firstprinciplesbasedpredictionof pages 8-11). These gaps directly support the PI's value proposition of coupling CALPHAD screening with experimental AM validation.

4. **GRX-810 yttria-content optimization (Chen et al., Jul 2026) narrows the design space for the secondary system.** The optimal window is 0.30–0.45 wt% Y₂O₃; above 0.5%, ductility degrades severely. This NASA co-authored result (with Gradl) is directly relevant to an AFOSR-aligned secondary demonstration (chen2026thecorrelationbetween pages 17-18, chen2026thecorrelationbetween pages 1-2).

5. **Elevated-temperature Al alloys for AM have advanced rapidly (Li et al., Nature Comms, Apr 2026).** A 582 MPa RT / 114 MPa at 400°C LPBF Al alloy with exceptional creep resistance at 400 °C sets a high benchmark for any bridge-system demonstration (li2026strongyetductile pages 1-6). ## Suggested Wording Changes for the White Paper

The current claim—*"This cost-aware, partial-evaluation formulation applied for the first time to a complex additive manufacturing pipeline for alloys is the core methodological novelty"*—should be revised in light of recent work demonstrating Bayesian multi-objective optimization for RHEA design (Islam et al., SSRN 7549378, Jan 2026), multi-fidelity active learning for TaNbMoVW (Jiang et al., J. Phys.: Mater. 9:025003, Feb 2026), closed-loop MPEA discovery (Priyadarshini et al., Mater. Horiz., Jul 2026), and LLNL's APEX autonomous DED platform (Mallia & Caputo, Aug 2026) (mallia2026aiguidedselfdrivinglaboratories pages 12-17, mallia2026aiguidedselfdrivinglaboratories pages 6-12).

**Suggested rewording:** *"While closed-loop Bayesian optimization and multi-fidelity surrogate strategies have recently been applied to alloy composition screening and individual AM process steps, no prior work has modeled the complete powder-to-elevated-temperature-property pipeline as a directed acyclic graph of heterogeneous surrogate nodes and optimized it via cost-aware Bayesian optimization of function networks with partial evaluations—where the algorithm autonomously decides when to query cheap nodes (CALPHAD simulations, single-track scans, density cubes, hardness maps) versus expensive terminal nodes (full elevated-temperature tensile/creep tests). This DAG-structured, partial-evaluation formulation applied to a physically executed, multi-stage additive manufacturing pipeline for refractory and superalloy systems is the core methodological novelty."*

This revision (i) acknowledges existing multi-fidelity and closed-loop work, (ii) specifies the DAG/BOFN/partial-evaluation architecture as the unique contribution, and (iii) ties the novelty to the physical AM pipeline rather than to computational-only optimization.

## Top 5 Things the PI Should Know

1. **The novelty claim needs tightening immediately.** At least three 2026 publications (Islam/Arroyave Bayesian multi-objective RHEA co-optimization; Jiang et al. multi-fidelity AL for TaNbMoVW; Priyadarshini et al. closed-loop MPEA discovery) use Bayesian or multi-fidelity optimization for complex alloy design. LLNL's APEX demonstrates a closed-loop DED-based alloy discovery platform. None, however, demonstrate cost-aware BOFN with partial evaluations across a physically executed multi-stage AM pipeline (powder → LPBF → microstructure → elevated-temperature property). The novelty claim must be narrowed to this specific DAG/partial-evaluation architecture.

2. **NASA's LDNb-ODS result (Brizes et al., Sep 2026) is the single most important refractory-AM benchmark.** It directly quantifies the performance gap the PI's platform should target: specific yield strength of 60–85 MPa/(g/cm³) to 800 °C, 10× improvement over C-103 in rupture at 1,093 °C, and oxidation as the life-limiting factor. This is from a NASA group (Smith, Kantzos) and should be cited in the one-pager.

3. **CALPHAD databases for refractory systems are expanding but remain incomplete.** Omprakash et al. generated DFT-informed pycalphad databases covering the full Cr-Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-V-W-Zr pool but lack liquidus/solidification data (omprakash2026firstprinciplesbasedpredictionof pages 8-11). Frey et al. emphasize missing interstitial (C, O) thermodynamics (frey2026aperspectiveon pages 28-30). These gaps directly support the PI's value proposition of coupling CALPHAD screening with experimental AM validation.

4. **GRX-810 yttria-content optimization (Chen et al., Jul 2026) narrows the design space for the secondary system.** The optimal window is 0.30–0.45 wt% Y₂O₃; above 0.5%, ductility degrades severely. This NASA co-authored result (with Gradl) is directly relevant to an AFOSR-aligned secondary demonstration (chen2026thecorrelationbetween pages 17-18, chen2026thecorrelationbetween pages 1-2).

5. **Elevated-temperature Al alloys for AM have advanced rapidly (Li et al., Nature Comms, Apr 2026).** A 582 MPa RT / 114 MPa at 400°C LPBF Al alloy with exceptional creep resistance at 400 °C sets a high benchmark for any bridge-system demonstration (li2026strongyetductile pages 1-6). The PI should frame the Al system as platform commissioning/validation, not an extreme-environment result per se.

## Suggested Wording Changes for the White Paper

The current claim—*"This cost-aware, partial-evaluation formulation applied for the first time to a complex additive manufacturing pipeline for alloys is the core methodological novelty"*—should be revised in light of recent work demonstrating Bayesian multi-objective optimization for RHEA design (Islam et al., SSRN 7549378, Jan 2026), multi-fidelity active learning for TaNbMoVW (Jiang et al., J. Phys.: Mater. 9:025003, Feb 2026), closed-loop MPEA discovery (Priyadarshini et al., Mater. Horiz., Jul 2026), and LLNL's APEX autonomous DED platform (Mallia & Caputo, Aug 2026) (mallia2026aiguidedselfdrivinglaboratories pages 12-17, mallia2026aiguidedselfdrivinglaboratories pages 6-12).

**Suggested rewording:** *"While closed-loop Bayesian optimization and multi-fidelity surrogate strategies have recently been applied to alloy composition screening and individual AM process steps, no prior work has modeled the complete powder-to-elevated-temperature-property pipeline as a directed acyclic graph of heterogeneous surrogate nodes and optimized it via cost-aware Bayesian optimization of function networks with partial evaluations—where the algorithm autonomously decides when to query cheap nodes (CALPHAD simulations, single-track scans, density cubes, hardness maps) versus expensive terminal nodes (full elevated-temperature tensile/creep tests). This DAG-structured, partial-evaluation formulation applied to a physically executed, multi-stage additive manufacturing pipeline for refractory and superalloy systems is the core methodological novelty."*

This revision (i) acknowledges existing multi-fidelity and closed-loop work, (ii) specifies the DAG/BOFN/partial-evaluation architecture as the unique contribution, and (iii) ties the novelty to the physical AM pipeline rather than to computational-only optimization.

(d) elevated-temperature aluminum alloys for AM (e.g., Al-Ce, Al-Zr-Sc-Er,
Al-Ni-Mn) that could serve as a low-melting-point bridge system for the
methodology demonstration, with aerospace-relevant service to ~300-400 C.
Highlight results that (i) make one demonstration system more or less
attractive for an AFOSR extreme-environments YIP, (ii) quantify current
performance gaps the platform should target (e.g., specific strength at
1200-1600 C, oxidation rate, room-temperature ductility thresholds,
crack-free LPBF windows), or (iii) come from AFRL, AFOSR-funded, NASA, or
DoD-laboratory groups.

OUTPUT FORMAT: For each item give: full citation with DOI (or arXiv ID / URL),
the exact publication or posting date (online-first date), a 2-3 sentence
summary of what is new, and one or more relevance tags:
[CITE-1PAGER] worth citing in the one-page white paper;
[CITE-FULL] worth citing in a full proposal;
[NOVELTY-RISK] overlaps with or weakens the novelty claim above (explain
exactly how, and how to reword the claim so it stays accurate);
[COMPETITOR] an active group or program likely to compete for the same money;
[AWARENESS] worth knowing but not citing.
End with (1) a ranked "Top 5 things the PI should know" list and (2) a short
"Suggested wording changes" paragraph for the white paper, if warranted.

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child

        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available

        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)

Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.

Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.

before.title: Before

Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: paper_search
info.description:
Search for papers in Google Scholar for you to look at.

Can be called repeatedly with identical parameters to retrieve more results (max 2 repeats).
A short summary of the retrieved papers will be returned, but to examine the full content of each paper,
you must use the gather_evidence tool.

query.description:
A Google Scholar search query, which can be a specific phrase, complete sentence,
or general keywords, e.g. 'machine learning for immunology'. Also can be
given search operators like 'author:'.
query.title: Query

min_year.description:
filter for minimum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
min_year.title: Min Year

max_year.description:
filter for maximum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
max_year.title: Max Year

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: CONTEXT (do not summarize this back): The PI (Sterling G. Baird, Assistant
Professor, Manufacturing Engineering, Brigham Young University; EXCLUDE the PI's
own publications from recommendations) is preparing a one-page pre-solicitation
white paper for the AFOSR Young Investigator Program (Aerospace Materials for
Extreme Environments portfolio, Program Officer Dr. Ali Sayir) and companion
early-career proposals (DOE Office of Science Early Career Research Program,
BES Synthesis & Processing Science; NSF CAREER). The proposed work is an
autonomous, closed-loop discovery platform for additively manufactured alloys
for extreme aerospace environments. The powder-to-property pipeline (CALPHAD ->
powder atomization -> laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) -> microstructure ->
elevated-temperature property) is modeled as a directed acyclic graph of
surrogate models and optimized by cost-aware, multi-fidelity Bayesian
optimization of function networks with partial evaluations (Buathong, Frazier
et al., ICML 2024; Astudillo & Frazier, NeurIPS 2021), so the algorithm decides
when to query cheap nodes (thermodynamic simulations; low-cost proxy
experiments such as single tracks, density cubes, hardness) versus expensive
nodes (full elevated-temperature tensile tests). CALPHAD screening uses
pycalphad / Thermo-Calc (TCHEA, TCNI). Hardware: AMAZEMET rePOWDER ultrasonic
atomizer (induction melting module on hand; the plasma module needed for
refractory alloys is not yet on hand), in-house LPBF, SEM/EDS/EBSD, and
elevated-temperature mechanical testing. Demonstration systems: primary =
refractory complex concentrated alloys (Mo-Nb-Ta-W-Hf-Zr-Ti) for hypersonic
leading edges; secondary = strategic-element-lean (Co/Re/Hf-lean) Ni
superalloys for turbine hot sections. Preliminary results: a working
multi-fidelity BOFN implementation, a CALPHAD pipeline, and a powder-to-part

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This review compiles and analyzes the current state of the art of modified high entropy alloys (MHEAs) processed by laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), establishing composition-processing-microstructure-property relationships that define their printability, structural integrity, and performance. After contextualizing HEA/MHEA concepts and LPBF‑specific solidification phenomena, the review places particular emphasis on the modification strategies that tailor phase stability, melt‑pool behavior, and processability. These include targeted alloying additions, principal‑element ratio adjustments, and microalloying routes to stabilize FCC/BCC/B2 phase composition, mitigate cracking, and enable precipitation strengthening or microstructural refinement under LPBF’s rapid thermal cycles. A second major focus is the correlation between these compositional modifications and the resulting mechanical properties in both the as‑built and post‑processed conditions. The compiled data reveals distinct strength-ductility regimes across Cantor‑type alloys, Al‑containing dual‑phase systems, and refractory BCC‑based MHEAs, demonstrating how specific elemental additions, phase engineering strategies, and post‑processing treatments modulate hardness, tensile behavior, elongation, and failure modes. The comparative analysis highlights the strong dependency of mechanical properties on controlled phase fractions, segregation behavior, precipitates distribution, and defects. Overall, this review shows that the successful deployment of LPBF‑processed MHEAs critically depends on composition‑aware process design, where alloy modification strategies and mechanical property requirements must be jointly optimized.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>In response to the elevated-temperature and weight-reduction demands of modern aerospace applications, a novel oxide-dispersion-strengthened low-density niobium alloy (LDNb-ODS) was fabricated using laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF). To overcome powder procurement barriers, L-PBF feedstock was produced by blending commercial Nb521, Ti64, and Cr powder with Y2O3 nanoparticles via resonant acoustic mixing. Following L-PBF and a 1400°C vacuum heat treatment, the alloy achieved a density of 6.73 g/cc and a fine mean grain size of 4.62 µm stabilized by uniform ~30 nm yttria dispersoids. Microstructural analysis revealed a chemically inhomogeneous build with lack-of-fusion defects and a titanium (Ti) shift from a nominal 31.5 wt% in the starting powder blend to 24.8 wt% in the printed part due to preferential Ti loss during printing. Elevated-temperature tensile testing demonstrated that LDNb-ODS maintained a superior specific yield strength of 60-85 MPa/(g/cc) up to 800°C, outperforming nickel-based alloys Ni625, Ni230, and GRX-810. Between 870°C and 950°C, its specific strength surpassed both Ni718 and Ni625. In rapid stress-rupture testing at 1093°C and 20.7 MPa, uncoated LDNb-ODS survived 21.4 hours (a tenfold increase over legacy C-103) while an R512E silicide coating extended rupture life to 84.8 hours, confirming that oxidation accelerates low-stress failure. These findings demonstrate that additive manufacturing of LDNb-ODS provides a viable, lightweight alternative to nickel-based superalloys for high-temperature (>850°C) aerospace components.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Hot isostatic pressing (HIP) is a critical post-processing step to ensure the reliability and performance of additively manufactured (AM) niobium (Nb) components for demanding aerospace and high-temperature applications. However, optimizing HIP cycles to maximize strength without relying on extensive and costly physical trials presents a significant industrial challenge. This work adapts a predictive phase-field modeling framework that directly correlates HIP process parameters of temperature and pressure to the final microstructure and mechanical strength of AM Nb, serving as a powerful tool for virtual process design. The simulation results provide quantitative guidance for manufacturing process design. The model demonstrates that applied pressure is a key lever for suppressing grain growth at high temperatures, thereby enhancing component strength. For instance, at a processing temperature of 1373 K, increasing the HIP pressure from 1 MPa to 100 MPa is predicted to boost the final yield strength by 5.70%. At a slightly lower temperature of 1273 K, the same pressure increase yields a significant 7.57% strength improvement. This critical link between processing, microstructure, and performance is established by coupling the predicted final grain size with the well-established Hall–Petch relation. This work enables manufacturers to reduce reliance on trial-and-error experimentation, accelerate the development of tailored heat treatment schedules, and reduce uncertainty in the final performance of critical components. The model establishes a foundation that can be extended to predict the behavior of more complex Nb-based alloys (e.g., C-103, Nb-1Zr), further enhancing its utility in the aerospace and advanced materials industries.</jats:p>

This review links the fundamentals of these materials to the data-driven methods now used to design them. The first part of this review describes the fundamentals of these materials, including the thermodynamic and kinetic basis of these materials and an entropy-based classification. The subsequent parts of this review describe the synthesis routes of these materials via liquid-state, solid-state, gas-state, and other processing routes. The choice of processing route can have a significant impact on the resulting material including the phase(s) formed, the chemical homogeneity, and contamination of the material. We have systematically reviewed the mechanical, corrosion, thermal, electrical, and soft magnetic properties of these HEAs. In the final section, we discuss how artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) can be used to solve the problem of combinatorial explosion of the design space of HEA: supervised classifiers for phase prediction, regression and ensemble models for hardness, strength, and elastic moduli, active learning and Bayesian optimization for closed loop discovery, high-throughput screening with CALPHAD and machine learned interatomic potentials. We conclude with continuing constraints such as lack of data, noisy labels, and poor encoding of process history, and areas of development including transfer learning, generative design, and self-driving laboratories. Machine learning-enabled discovery of refractory high entropy alloys on curated data Valid Text Names: 'yan2026machinelearningenableddiscovery pages 1-5', 'yan2026machinelearningenableddiscovery pages 5-10', 'yan2026machinelearningenableddiscovery pages 10-14', 'yan2026machinelearningenableddiscovery pages 14-19', 'yan2026machinelearningenableddiscovery pages 19-22', 'yan2026machinelearningenableddiscovery pages 22-25', 'yan2026machinelearningenableddiscovery pages 25-27', 'yan2026machinelearningenableddiscovery pages 27-30' BibTex: @article{yan2026machinelearningenableddiscovery, author = "Yan, Yonggang and Zhou, Nan and Liao, Yalin and Cui, Lijuan and dahuan Zhu and Hu, Xunxiang", title = "Machine learning-enabled discovery of refractory high entropy alloys on curated data", url = "https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10354540/v1", doi = "10.21203/rs.3.rs-10354540/v1", publisher = "Springer Science and Business Media LLC", year = "2026", month = "Aug", journal = "Unknown journal" } Abstract: Abstract

Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) exhibit outstanding potential for high-temperature structural applications, yet their rational design remains challenging because of the enormous compositional space and inconsistent literature data. Herein, we develop a machine-learning framework for predicting phase stability using a carefully curated RHEA dataset that combines secondary phase-inspired descriptors, refined synthesis metadata, and reassessed phase labels. The resulting ML model achieves a high predictive performance (F1 score = 0.89) in identifying single-phase solid solution RHEAs. Model interpretation reveals a key finding: RHEAs with a mismatch in the most stable oxidation state among constituent elements (MSO_dv) substantially exceeding 15 are prone to forming ordered intermetallic phases, thereby compromising single-phase stability. Theoretical analysis further links MSO to the itinerant electron characteristics of elements, elucidating the electronic origin of its impact on phase formation. Additionally, factors such as annealing temperature and first ionization energy are also shown to govern phase formation by modulating multiphase solid solution formation. Guided by ML predictions, several RHEAs were successfully synthesized and validated experimentally. This study establishes a robust predictive framework and unveils previously unrecognized electronic mechanisms, offering a new paradigm for the rational discovery of high-performance RHEAs.

Target-driven discovery of metal hydrides using a high-throughput computational framework: from operational targets to sustainability assessment Valid Text Names: 'strozi2026targetdrivendiscoveryof pages 1-2', 'strozi2026targetdrivendiscoveryof pages 2-3', 'strozi2026targetdrivendiscoveryof pages 3-4', 'strozi2026targetdrivendiscoveryof pages 4-5', 'strozi2026targetdrivendiscoveryof pages 5-6', 'strozi2026targetdrivendiscoveryof pages 6-7', 'strozi2026targetdrivendiscoveryof pages 7-8', 'strozi2026targetdrivendiscoveryof pages 8-10', 'strozi2026targetdrivendiscoveryof pages 10-11', 'strozi2026targetdrivendiscoveryof pages 11-12', 'strozi2026targetdrivendiscoveryof pages 12-13', 'strozi2026targetdrivendiscoveryof pages 13-14', 'strozi2026targetdrivendiscoveryof pages 14-14' BibTex: @article{strozi2026targetdrivendiscoveryof, author = "Strozi, Renato Belli and Stoco, Caroline Binde and Pedroso, Otávio Abreu and Coury, Francisco Gil and Campello, Betania and Floriano, Ricardo and Zepon, Guilherme", title = "Target-driven discovery of metal hydrides using a high-throughput computational framework: from operational targets to sustainability assessment", year = "2026", journal = "npj Computational Materials", month = "Aug", doi = "10.1038/s41524-026-02295-4", url = "https://doi.org/10.1038/s41524-026-02295-4", publisher = "Springer Science and Business Media LLC", issn = "2057-3960" } Abstract: Abstract Metal hydrides based on multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) offer tunable hydrogen storage properties, but their vast compositional space poses significant design challenges. A high-throughput computational strategy is proposed to identify alloys under predefined operating conditions, demonstrated here for hydrogen gas separation. CALPHAD equilibrium calculations were performed in the Ti-V-Cr-Nb system using a Python TM script with PanPython (Pandat TM SDK). Superalloys have exceptional properties such as resistance to creep and thermal fatigue, mechanical strength at high temperatures, resistance to corrosion and oxidation, and resistance to phase separation with time. Superalloys are primarily based on nickel (Ni), but cobalt (Co)-based and iron (Fe)-nickel-based variants are also available. Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>In this paper, laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) prepared GRX-810 samples with different yttria contents (from 0.3 to 1 wt%) were systematically examined. The mechanical properties and thermal properties were measured under as-built and Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP) heat treated conditions. The results indicate that yttria content significantly affects the thermal properties of as-built L-PBF GRX-810. Higher yttria reduces thermal diffusivity and conductivity by up to 6% in of as-built samples. HIP restores thermal properties to low-yttria levels, indicating that L-PBF-induced microdefects and porosity, rather than composition, primarily cause the thermal degradation. Based on the mechanical testing results, yttria content up to 0.45% provides the most favorable strength–ductility balance in the present dataset. Higher yttria content (from 0.5 to 1%) leads to the reduction of the elongation from 27% to around 4% in the as-built samples. Following HIP, the yield strength decreases from ~ 785 MPa in the as-built state to ~ 685 MPa. The elongation increases from 4% in the as-built state to ~ 42%. HIP samples with yttria content less than 0.45% exhibit a high ductility at approximately 40% maximum elongation, while HIP samples with yttria content higher than 0.5% exhibit a moderate ductility of approximately 18% maximum elongation at failure. These thermal and mechanical performance studies provide valuable guidance for GRX-810 applications and provide a reference for further AM-ODS alloy optimization.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The nature of stacking faults (SF) – whether intrinsic or extrinsic – plays a pivotal role in defect-mediated processes in crystalline materials. Yet, transmission electron microscopy (TEM) techniques for their reliable analysis remain limited to either conventional fringe-contrast imaging of inclined faults or atomic-resolution imaging of edge-on configurations. Here, we overcome this long-standing geometric constraint by introducing a high-resolution scanning TEM method that enables full structural discrimination of inclined SFs, as demonstrated in fcc, L1₂, and sphalerite crystals. This approach complements edge-on analysis and provides access to SFs on all glide planes along commonly utilized zone axes. We demonstrate the method’s robustness in a CoNi-based superalloy by discriminating fault types even in overlapping configurations and for foil thicknesses exceeding 100 nm, and extend its application to analyzing bounding partial dislocations in inclined geometries to reveal the fault formation mechanism. Probe propagation simulations reveal that fault-induced de-channeling is key to contrast formation and is strongly governed by the fault’s depth within the sample. Leveraging this effect, we further establish a route to artificially generate ultrathin TEM lamellae – bounded by the SF itself – enhancing contrast for atomic-scale studies of long-range ordering and compositional fluctuations.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Discovering new high-performance materials and alloys is often likened to finding a needle in a haystack because the design space of chemical compositions and processing conditions is astronomically large, and the discovery process is laborious and prohibitively costly. This perspective articulates a research agenda for autonomous materials and metallurgy discovery platforms that combine closed-loop machine learning with robotic experimentation and traditional materials engineering precepts to formulate, process, and test candidate materials with reduced human intervention, and to iterate recursively for stepwise optimization. It explores how sequential learning methods, generative modeling, and hybrid model-based strategies can analyze multimodal experimental data and propose new compositions and processing schedules for subsequent experiments. This approach has the potential to considerably accelerate the pace of discoveries, from decades to mere weeks. Representation learning for material formulations, the injection of domain knowledge into decision-making, and the mechatronic design of robotics that can safely execute harsh processing are all explored as essential components in closing the autonomous loop. Surveyed exemplars show order-of-magnitude improvements in experimental throughput and discovery efficiency. Furthermore, the paper proposes a multidimensional framework for classifying and evaluating the autonomy, complexity, and integration levels of self-driving laboratories, intended to give researchers and practitioners a structured approach to benchmarking future developments in the field. The perspective concludes with an analysis of data infrastructure, simulation coupling, robustness, and human-machine collaboration, distilled into a structured research agenda whose pursuit would broaden adoption across energy, aerospace, and other sectors.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Additive manufacturing (AM) is revolutionizing the aerospace, transportation, energy, and biomedical fields due to its capacity for rapid production of geometrically complex components. The advancement of alloys for AM is critical to further boost those applications. The first-generation alloys for AM largely rely on conventional commercial alloys that were originally developed under the assumption of near-equilibrium solidification. However, some of these materials are incompatible with the non-equilibrium metallurgical behavior of AM, which may face issues like high crack susceptibility. Thus, the second-generation alloy design for AM builds upon conventional alloy systems by inoculation treatments with alloying elements (e.g., zirconium) or ceramic reinforcements (e.g., titanium carbide) to achieve better material printability and properties. Meanwhile, the limitations of commercial materials underscore the need for developing novel alloys specifically tailored for AM. The third-generation empirical approach for material design adopts a knowledge-driven strategy by leveraging established metallurgical principles and empirical correlations to guide targeted composition optimization. Such trial-and-error strategies for discovering new materials face substantial bottlenecks like long development cycles and high costs. Hence, it has propelled research toward the fourth-generation paradigm—data-driven artificial intelligence (AI) assisted materials design for AM, which is an effective and innovative material solution guided by AM-specific metallurgical features. Advances in AI and robotics will shift the future paradigm of AM-specific alloy design toward an autonomous AI-Lab, which leverages an intelligent AM agent and automated high-throughput AM printing and testing for materials discovery.</jats:p>
