Efficient exploration of vast compositional and processing spaces is essential for accelerated materials discovery. Bayesian optimization (BO) provides a principled strategy for identifying optimal materials with minimal experiments, yet its adoption in materials science ishindered by implementation complexity and limited domain-specific tools. Here, we presentBgolearn, a comprehensive Python framework that makes BO accessible and practical for materials research through an intuitive interface, robust algorithms, and materials-oriented workflows. Bgolearn supports both single-objective and multi-objective Bayesian optimization withmultiple acquisition functions (e.g., expected improvement, upper confidence bound, probability of improvement, and expected hypervolume improvement etc.), diverse surrogate models(including Gaussian processes, random forests, and gradient boosting etc.), and bootstrapbased uncertainty quantification. Benchmark studies show that Bgolearn reduces the numberof required experiments by 40–60% compared with random search, grid search, and geneticalgorithms, while maintaining comparable or superior solution quality. Its effectiveness isdemonstrated not only through the studies presented in this paper, such as the identificationof maximum-elastic-modulus triply periodic minimal surface structures, ultra-high-hardnesshigh-entropy alloys, and high-strength, high-ductility medium-Mn steels, but also by numerous publications that have proven its impact in material discovery. With a modular architecture that integrates seamlessly into existing materials workflows and a graphical user interface (BgoFace) that removes programming barriers, Bgolearn establishes a practical andreliable platform for Bayesian optimization in materials science, and is openly available athttps://github.com/Bin-Cao/Bgolearn.

Machine Learning in Materials Science: Data-Driven Discovery and Functional Applications Valid Text Names: 'kolev2026machinelearningin pages 1-2', 'kolev2026machinelearningin pages 2-4', 'kolev2026machinelearningin pages 4-6', 'kolev2026machinelearningin pages 6-7', 'kolev2026machinelearningin pages 7-9', 'kolev2026machinelearningin pages 9-10', 'kolev2026machinelearningin pages 10-12', 'kolev2026machinelearningin pages 12-13', 'kolev2026machinelearningin pages 13-15', 'kolev2026machinelearningin pages 15-16', 'kolev2026machinelearningin pages 16-18', 'kolev2026machinelearningin pages 18-20', 'kolev2026machinelearningin pages 20-21', 'kolev2026machinelearningin pages 21-22' BibTex: @article{kolev2026machinelearningin, author = "Kolev, Mihail", title = "Machine Learning in Materials Science: Data-Driven Discovery and Functional Applications", year = "2026", journal = "Encyclopedia", volume = "6", pages = "150", month = "Jul", doi = "10.3390/encyclopedia6070150", url = "https://doi.org/10.3390/encyclopedia6070150", publisher = "MDPI AG", issue = "7", issn = "2673-8392" } Abstract: Machine learning (ML) in materials science refers to computational methods that learn statistical, structural, or physics-informed relationships from experimental, computational, and literature-derived materials data. These methods are used to predict materials properties, identify structure–property and process–structure–property–performance relationships, discover candidate materials, optimize synthesis and processing routes, and guide functional applications. ML is narrower than artificial intelligence (AI), which also includes broader reasoning, planning, search, and automation capabilities. It is also distinct from materials informatics, which is the wider data-centered framework that includes databases, descriptors, metadata, workflows, visualization, and knowledge management. ML can complement high-throughput computation by building surrogate models from density functional theory, finite-element simulation, molecular dynamics, or experimental data, but it is not identical to high-throughput screening itself. Unlike conventional physics-based modeling, which begins with explicit governing equations or mechanistic assumptions, ML usually infers predictive relationships from data; modern approaches increasingly combine both perspectives through physics-informed features, uncertainty quantification, and human expertise. Lightweight Al alloys capable of retaining mechanical performance at elevated temperatures are increasingly relevant for transportation and structural applications. Al-Ce alloys are particularly attractive because of their good castability and thermally stable Ce-containing intermetallics. However, how Cr addition modifies phase formation and mechanical behavior under rapid solidification remains insufficiently understood. This study investigates the processing–microstructure–property relationships of Al–13Ce and Al–10Ce–1Cr (wt%) alloys produced by centrifugal solidification (CS), with directional solidification (DS) used for comparison. CS was performed using a stepped Cu mold with bulk diameters of 5–11 mm, and the resulting alloys were characterized by SEM/EDS, XRD, Vickers microhardness, and compression testing. CS produced markedly refined microstructures, with dendritic spacings of approximately 4.0–5.4 µm. The Al–13Ce alloy exhibited a cellular-to-dendritic transition corresponding to samples having smaller diameters, whereas Al–10Ce–1Cr retained a dendritic morphology throughout all conditions. The Cr-containing alloy generally exhibited higher compressive and yield strengths, reaching 282 and 143 MPa, respectively, compared with 253 and 119 MPa for Al–13Ce in the same 11-mm CS condition. The Hollomon analysis revealed a higher strength coefficient (K) but lower strain-hardening exponent (n) for Al–10Ce–1Cr, indicating higher resistance to plastic flow but a reduced strain-hardening capacity, consistent with the presence of primary Al 20 CeCr 2 particles. Overall, the compressive response was governed not only by microstructural refinement but also by phase constitution, intermetallic distribution, and particle/matrix interactions, highlighting the combined roles of alloy chemistry and solidification route in tailoring Al-Ce-based alloys.

D.", title = "Mechanical and in situ thermal-related behavior during directed energy deposition additive manufacturing of a high-performance Al alloy", year = "2026", journal = "International Journal of Extreme Manufacturing", volume = "8", pages = "035002", month = "Jan", doi = "10.1088/2631-7990/ae3349", url = "https://doi.org/10.1088/2631-7990/ae3349", publisher = "IOP Publishing", issue = "3", issn = "2631-8644" } Abstract: Abstract Directed energy deposition (DED) additive manufacturing (AM) can fabricate, repair, and join near-net-shaped components for high-performance engineering applications, including biomedical, energy, and transport sectors. The broader adoption of DED remains constrained by the limited number of alloys available that can be reliably manufactured without imperfections, hence limiting mechanical properties. Here, we designed an Al–Ni–Ce–Mn–Fe AM alloy that can achieve an ultra-fine microstructure (<5 μm), uniform distribution of intermetallics, low residual stress (<32 MPa), and superior mechanical properties in as-built DED components. Compared to DED AlSi10Mg in the as-built state using the same conditions, the yield increased by 70%, and the ultimate tensile strength by 50%. DED-AM involves rapid cooling and complex thermal conditions, which largely influence the property of the final components. Post-characterization cannot capture the time resolved thermal behavior, hence offer limited mechanism-based guide for alloy design. In this study, we develop a novel multimodal characterization methodology for correlative in situ X-ray imaging, X-ray diffraction, and infrared imaging, enabling quantification of the in situ thermal-related behavior, including phase evolution, temperature distribution, and stress accumulation during DED. We elucidated key mechanisms driving the structure refinement and stress development in this alloy. The insights gained into the interplay between alloy composition, thermal-related behavior, and performance under specific AM conditions inform next-generation material design tailored for AM technologies.                   <jats:p>Titanium-based medium entropy alloys (MEAs) have emerged as a promising class of materials for high-temperature applications because of their distinct combination of superior mechanical characteristics, oxidation resistance, and thermal stability. This review explores the fabrication techniques, microstructural features and mechanical performance of titanium-based MEAs, highlighting their potential in industries such as energy, automotive, and aerospace. Alloying elements are discussed in terms of their influence on the mechanical strength, creep resistance, and phase stability of these alloys. The review also examines the role of various fabrication methods, including arc melting, powder metallurgy, additive manufacturing, and mechanical alloying, in tailoring the microstructure and enhancing the performance of titanium-based MEAs. Challenges in fabricating titanium-based MEAs. Furthermore, the review highlights emerging trends in MEA research, including alloy optimization, surface modification strategies, and the integration of computational modelling and machine learning. Despite the promising advantages, significant research is required to overcome the current limitations and further enhance the performance and sustainability of titanium-based MEAs for high-temperature applications.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>High-wear-resistant iron-based clad layers demonstrate substantial application potential in aerospace, automotive, and industrial equipment due to their excellent mechanical properties and extended service life. Laser cladding has emerged as a pivotal technology for the additive manufacturing and repair of critical components, characterized by rapid cooling rates, narrow heat-affected zones, and dense microstructures. However, fabricating high-wear-resistant Fe-based clad layers remains challenging, particularly in achieving a trade-off among hardness, wear resistance, and toughness. Excessively high hardness often compromises toughness, increasing susceptibility to cracking and reducing service reliability, whereas insufficient hardness undermines functional performance and shortens service life. This review synthesizes recent advances in microstructural design, control, and optimization of high-wear-resistant Fe-based clad layers, focusing on powder alloying design, process parameter optimization, and post-cladding strengthening treatments. The strengthening mechanisms and performance characteristics of key alloying elements, specifically Cr, B, Nb, Mo, and Ti, are summarized, and the effects of laser power, scanning speed, and powder feeding rate on the microstructure and properties are systematically discussed. Furthermore, the influence of post-treatment processes, including turning, grinding, ultrasonic rolling, and heat treatment, on wear resistance enhancement is also addressed. Finally, future development directions for laser cladding of high-wear-resistant Fe-based clad layers are proposed.</jats:p>

messages.content:
Most relevant evidence (with ids):

## pqac-00000040

From text 'ray2026universalelectronicmanifolds pages 8-9'.

Pranoy Ray, Sayan Bhowmik, Phanish Suryanarayana, Surya R. Kalidindi, and Andrew J. Medford. Electronic manifolds for extrapolative alloy discovery. Digital Discovery, Mar 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2603.06953, doi:10.48550/arxiv.2603.06953. This article has 2 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

Ray et al. describe a transferable electronic-manifold framework for extrapolative discovery in refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The method represents alloys using a pseudo-electron-density descriptor based on the superposition of atomic charges, rather than the fully converged DFT density. PCA shows that this descriptor recovers the trapezoidal geometry of the four-element composition/structure space and that four- and seven-component alloy datasets occupy overlapping manifolds. This suggests that local electronic packing environments, rather than explicit elemental identities alone, support transfer to elements absent from training. The approach removes the self-consistent-field (SCF) bottleneck from descriptor generation and is combined with Gaussian-process regression and Bayesian active learning. A model trained on 200 samples from the four-component Al-Nb-Ti-Zr domain demonstrated zero-shot predictive power for five-, six-, and seven-component alloys containing unseen Mo, Ta, V, and W. Few-shot adaptation using only 20 actively selected target-domain samples achieved NMAEs of 5.54% (R²=0.85) for five-component alloys, 4.16% for six-component alloys, and 2.87% (R²=0.68) for seven-component alloys. For in-domain bulk-modulus screening, fewer than 2% NMAE was achieved with 10 actively selected samples, indicating substantial sample and computational efficiency.


---

## pqac-00000041

From text 'ray2026universalelectronicmanifolds pages 5-6'.

Pranoy Ray, Sayan Bhowmik, Phanish Suryanarayana, Surya R. Kalidindi, and Andrew J. Medford. Electronic manifolds for extrapolative alloy discovery. Digital Discovery, Mar 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2603.06953, doi:10.48550/arxiv.2603.06953. This article has 2 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

Ray et al. describe an electronic-manifold approach for extrapolative discovery in refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The method constructs spatial autocorrelation descriptors from unrelaxed, superposed pseudo-valence-electron densities generated from elemental pseudopotentials, avoiding the self-consistent-field (SCF) calculations needed to obtain converged charge densities. These descriptors encode chemically meaningful electronic structure and place related refractory transition metals in a continuously connected feature space, enabling regression across compositions rather than interpolation among disconnected clusters. A Gaussian process regression (GPR) model predicts composition-averaged properties, while active learning uses predictive uncertainty to select candidates for expensive DFT labeling. Training on the lower-order Al–Nb–Ti–Zr domain (D4) and testing without retraining on the refractory D7 domain (Mo–Nb–Ta–Ti–V–W–Zr) provides a zero-shot extrapolation test. For bulk modulus, active learning reaches normalized mean absolute error (NMAE) below 2% with only 10 total training samples (four random seeds plus six active acquisitions), compared with roughly 26 samples for converged-density descriptors and much larger datasets for typical methods. Even random sampling achieves R² = 0.98 and MAE = 1.41 GPa on D4, indicating strong global correlation and substantially reduced feature-generation cost.


---

## pqac-00000042

From text 'ray2026universalelectronicmanifolds pages 1-2'.

Pranoy Ray, Sayan Bhowmik, Phanish Suryanarayana, Surya R. Kalidindi, and Andrew J. Medford. Electronic manifolds for extrapolative alloy discovery. Digital Discovery, Mar 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2603.06953, doi:10.48550/arxiv.2603.06953. This article has 2 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

Ray et al. describe an efficient, physics-informed framework for extrapolative discovery in refractory high-entropy alloys. Instead of using expensive self-consistent DFT charge densities, the method uses a non-interacting valence electron pseudo-density: a superposition of isolated atomic valence densities placed on Special Quasirandom Structure lattice sites, with geometry set using Vegard’s Law and no subsequent electronic relaxation. Directionally resolved two-point spatial correlations encode the pseudo-density’s structural and electronic information, and Principal Component Analysis compresses these features. {"answer": "# Extreme-Environment Alloys by Additive Manufacturing: Developments April–October 2026

This report synthesizes new work published or posted between 2026-04-01 and 2026-10-06 across four sub-topics relevant to the PI's proposed autonomous alloy discovery platform for AM extreme-environment alloys. Items from January–March 2026 are included only when especially important and are labeled "earlier 2026." Several highly relevant papers were identified but could not be obtained for full-text verification; these are flagged accordingly.

The summary table below organizes the most consequential items by topic, relevance tag, and actionable significance.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

---

## (a) Refractory Complex Concentrated Alloys and Nb-Based Alloys Processed by AM

**Brizes, E. et al., "A Dispersion-Strengthened Low-Density Niobium Alloy and Its Elevated Temperature Mechanical Performance," NASA Technical Report, Sep 2026. DOI: 10.64631/zcym1460**
Online: September 2026. NASA GRC/AFRL-relevant team fabricated an oxide-dispersion-strengthened low-density Nb alloy (LDNb-ODS) by LPBF from blended Nb521 + Ti64 + Cr + Y₂O₃ nanoparticle powder. Density was 6.73 g/cm³ with ~30 nm yttria dispersoids. Room-temperature UTS reached 1,005 MPa; specific yield strength of 60–85 MPa/(g/cm³) was maintained to 800 °C, surpassing Ni625, Ni230, and GRX-810 in that regime. At 1,093 °C/20.7 MPa, uncoated LDNb-ODS survived 21.4 h (10× legacy C-103), while R512E silicide coating extended life to 84.8 h. Oxidation—not creep—was the dominant life-limiting mechanism. Lack-of-fusion defects and Ti volatilization (31.5→24.8 wt%) were identified as processability challenges (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000003). **Tags: [CITE-1PAGER] [CITE-FULL] [COMPETITOR]** — This NASA result directly quantifies the performance gap the PI's platform should target and validates LPBF of Nb-based ODS alloys.

**Keller, T. et al., "Additive manufacturing of refractory niobium alloys: a review," Progress in Additive Manufacturing, 11:6491–6517, May 2026. DOI: 10.1007/s40964-026-01728-2**
Online: May 2026. Comprehensive review of AM Nb alloy processing covering LPBF and EB-PBF. Highlights that oxygen pickup can drive Nb ductility to nearly zero at ~1 at.% O, underscoring the importance of atmosphere control and powder handling throughout the pipeline (pqac-00000004). **Tags: [CITE-FULL]**

**Jabir, A.A.M. et al., "Investigation of process parameters to fabricate TiWMo refractory medium entropy alloy via LPBF," Progress in Additive Manufacturing, 11:5567–5577, Mar 2026. DOI: 10.1007/s40964-026-01648-1** *(earlier 2026)*
Online: March 2026. Elemental-blend LPBF of equimolar TiWMo produced a single BCC phase with 633 HV max hardness. Fine W powder (5–25 µm) at 350 W / 250 mm/s reduced unmelted W to 0.01%. Demonstrates a low-cost composition-screening route from elemental powders but does not report tensile ductility or elevated-temperature properties (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000038). **Tags: [CITE-FULL]**

**Rubio-Ejchel, D. et al., "Laser powder directed energy deposition fabrication and tensile sandwich evaluation of Ti64-C103-GRCop-42 functionally graded materials," J. Mater. Res., Sep 2026. DOI: 10.1557/s43578-026-01964-w**
Online: September 2026. CALPHAD/Scheil-informed LP-DED grading with C103 as intermediate bridge: Ti64→C103 gradient achieved >99% density and 390 MPa yield / 510 MPa UTS / ~45% local elongation in C103, but Cu–Hf intermetallics caused brittle failure at the C103→GRCop-42 interface (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000048, pqac-00000052). **Tags: [CITE-FULL]**

**Dodge, B.S. et al., "Ultrasonic atomization of a refractory high-entropy alloy TiZrNbHfTa for additive manufacturing," Powders, 5:25, Jul 2026. DOI: 10.3390/powders5030025** *(unobtainable — full-text verification needed)*
Directly relevant to the PI's rePOWDER ultrasonic atomizer: establishes ultrasonic atomization of a quinary refractory HEA. **Tags: [CITE-1PAGER] [CITE-FULL]**

**Xiao, B. et al., "Microstructure and mechanical properties of WMoTaNbV refractory high-entropy alloy via electron-beam powder-bed fusion," Appl. Mater. Today, 52:103378, Oct 2026. DOI: 10.1016/j.apmt.2026.103378** *(unobtainable)*
Timely EB-PBF data on the canonical W-Mo-Ta-Nb-V system. **Tags: [CITE-FULL]**

**Sowards, J.W. et al., "Solidification cracking of refractory alloys: a computational and machine learning study," Materials & Design, 263:115679, Mar 2026. DOI: 10.1016/j.matdes.2026.115679** *(earlier 2026, unobtainable)*
ML-based composition-dependent cracking prediction for refractory AM. Partially overlaps the proposed cheap-printability-surrogate node. **Tags: [CITE-1PAGER] [CITE-FULL] [NOVELTY-RISK] [COMPETITOR]** — The PI should position such models as constituent nodes within the DAG, not claim novelty of ML for refractory cracking prediction per se.

**Kumaravel, M. et al., "Mitigating the challenges in AM of refractory CCAs using Ti alloying via multi-material feedstock," MSEA, Jan 2026. DOI: 10.1016/j.msea.2026.149867** *(earlier 2026, unobtainable)*
Ti alloying as a ductilization strategy for RCCA LPBF. **Tags: [CITE-FULL]**

**Frey, C. et al., "A Perspective on the Historical and Contemporary Development of Refractory Alloys," Met. Mater. Trans. A, 57:461–503, 2026 issue. DOI: 10.1007/s11661-025-07996-x**
Identifies key gaps: minimum low-temperature ductility/toughness for crack-free printing is unknown; partition coefficients and solidus/liquidus data are sparse; current CALPHAD databases typically omit interstitial elements (C, O) despite their critical effects on cracking and ductility (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000026). **Tags: [AWARENESS]** — Treat as outside the primary window unless online-first date confirmed in 2026.

---

## (b) ML- or CALPHAD-Guided Design of RCCAs

**Ray, P. et al., "Electronic manifolds for extrapolative alloy discovery," Digital Discovery, Mar 2026. DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2603.06953** *(earlier 2026)*
Physics-informed pseudo-electron-density descriptors enable Bayesian active learning that predicts bulk modulus with <2% NMAE from only 10 training samples (~0.2% of dataset) in the Al-Nb-Ti-Zr space, and transfers zero-shot to the 7-component Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-V-W-Zr system; 20 actively selected target samples yield <3% NMAE (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000042). Demonstrates radical sample efficiency for RCCA property prediction. **Tags: [CITE-1PAGER] [CITE-FULL]**

**Peterson, N.E. et al., "Machine Learning Guided CALPHAD Design of Ru-Stabilized BCC B2 Refractory Alloys," arXiv:2609.14925, Sep 2026.**
Random-forest active learning coupled to Thermo-Calc TCHEA4 screened 500 compositions in the Nb-Ta-Mo-V-Ru-Ti-Zr-Hf-Al-Y space, identifying 100 meeting BCC+B2 stability, phase purity, and precipitate-fraction criteria at 1300 °C. Promising Nb-Mo-Ti-Ru-Hf-Zr and Nb-Ta-Ru-Hf compositions identified (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030). **Tags: [CITE-FULL] [COMPETITOR]**

**Omprakash, P. et al., "First-principles-based Prediction of Phase Fields: Part I. Binary and Ternary Refractory Alloys," arXiv:2609.06627, Sep 2026.**
DFT-informed pycalphad databases cover the full Cr-Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-V-W-Zr element pool, generating phase diagrams for 36 binaries through 126 quinaries. Liquidus data remain absent, making experimental solidification benchmarks valuable. This directly validates the PI's pycalphad pipeline and identifies where that pipeline adds value (pqac-00000025). **Tags: [CITE-FULL]**

**Shen, C. et al., "How Can Machine Learning Accelerate CALPHAD Free Energy Modeling?" arXiv:2606.01305, May 2026.**
Proposes ML surrogates for CALPHAD Gibbs energy functions spanning transition metals and refractory elements. **Tags: [AWARENESS]**

**Yan, Y. et al., "Machine learning-enabled discovery of refractory high entropy alloys on curated data," Research Square preprint, Aug 2026. DOI: 10.21203/rs.3.rs-10354540/v1**
Curated RHEA dataset with phase-label reassessment; F1=0.89 for predicting single-phase BCC stability, identifying mismatch in most-stable oxidation state (MSO_dv > 15) as a new ordering descriptor. **Tags: [CITE-FULL]**

**Islam, M.S. et al. / Arroyave group, "Bayesian multi-objective co-optimization of performance and manufacturability in BCC-B2 refractory high entropy alloys," SSRN 7549378, Jan 2026.** *(earlier 2026, unobtainable)*
**Tags: [NOVELTY-RISK] [COMPETITOR] [CITE-FULL]** — This work explicitly combines Bayesian multi-objective optimization with manufacturability constraints for RHEAs. It overlaps the PI's claim of "first" Bayesian optimization for AM RCCA pipelines. DED of an Al-Ni-Ce-Mn-Fe alloy using ultrasonic-atomized powder achieved <5 µm microstructure, <32 MPa residual stress, and 70%/50% improvements in yield/UTS over DED AlSi10Mg. LPBF of an Al-Ce-Fe-Ni-Zr alloy — directly in the compositional space of interest for elevated-temperature Al alloys. **Tags: [CITE-FULL]**

---

## Novelty Risk and Competitor Assessment

**LLNL APEX** — The Autonomous Alloy Prediction and Experimentation platform is a DED-based self-driving laboratory integrating robotic handling, post-processing, and automated characterization (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033). It is classified as {MSS-3 (bulk metallurgy), HAL-2 (linked modules), SAL-2 (reactive closed-loop BO)}. Available evidence does not show it using BOFN, partial-evaluation fidelity management, or cost-aware node-selection decisions. **Tags: [COMPETITOR] [NOVELTY-RISK]** — APEX weakens generic "first autonomous AM alloy platform" claims but does not preempt the specific BOFN/partial-evaluation methodology.

**Priyadarshini, M.S. et al., "Machine learning-driven closed-loop discovery of hard multiple principal element alloys," Materials Horizons, Jul 2026. DOI: 10.1039/d6mh00103c** *(unobtainable)*
**Tags: [NOVELTY-RISK] [COMPETITOR]** — Closed-loop MPEA discovery. Blocks a blanket "first closed-loop complex-alloy discovery" claim.

**Zhao, L. et al., "Alloy design paradigms in additive manufacturing," Int. J. Extreme Manuf., 8:033003, Mar 2026. DOI: 10.1088/2631-7990/ae45de** *(earlier 2026)*
Proposes an "AI Auto-Lab for AM Materials" paradigm (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000034). Although primarily a roadmap, it makes generic "first autonomous AM alloy platform" language untenable. **Tags: [AWARENESS] [NOVELTY-RISK]**

---

## Top 5 Things the PI Should Know

1. **The novelty claim needs tightening immediately.** At least three 2026 publications (Islam/Arroyave Bayesian multi-objective RHEA co-optimization; Jiang et al. multi-fidelity AL for TaNbMoVW; Priyadarshini et al. closed-loop MPEA discovery) use Bayesian or multi-fidelity optimization for complex alloy design. LLNL's APEX demonstrates a closed-loop DED-based alloy discovery platform. None, however, demonstrate cost-aware BOFN with partial evaluations across a physically executed multi-stage AM pipeline (powder → LPBF → microstructure → elevated-temperature property). The novelty claim must be narrowed to this specific DAG/partial-evaluation architecture.

2. **NASA's LDNb-ODS result (Brizes et al., Sep 2026) is the single most important refractory-AM benchmark.** It directly quantifies the performance gap the PI's platform should target: specific yield strength of 60–85 MPa/(g/cm³) to 800 °C, 10× improvement over C-103 in rupture at 1,093 °C, and oxidation as the life-limiting factor. This is from a NASA group (Smith, Kantzos) and should be cited in the one-pager.

3. **CALPHAD databases for refractory systems are expanding but remain incomplete.** Omprakash et al. generated DFT-informed pycalphad databases covering the full Cr-Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-V-W-Zr pool but lack liquidus/solidification data (pqac-00000025). Frey et al. emphasize missing interstitial (C, O) thermodynamics (pqac-00000026). These gaps directly support the PI's value proposition of coupling CALPHAD screening with experimental AM validation.

4. **GRX-810 yttria-content optimization (Chen et al., Jul 2026) narrows the design space for the secondary system.** The optimal window is 0.30–0.45 wt% Y₂O₃; above 0.5%, ductility degrades severely. This NASA co-authored result (with Gradl) is directly relevant to an AFOSR-aligned secondary demonstration (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009).

5. **Elevated-temperature Al alloys for AM have advanced rapidly (Li et al., Nature Comms, Apr 2026).** A 582 MPa RT / 114 MPa at 400°C LPBF Al alloy with exceptional creep resistance at 400 °C sets a high benchmark for any bridge-system demonstration (pqac-00000017). The PI should frame the Al system as platform commissioning/validation, not an extreme-environment result per se.

---

## Suggested Wording Changes for the White Paper

The current claim—*"This cost-aware, partial-evaluation formulation applied for the first time to a complex additive manufacturing pipeline for alloys is the core methodological novelty"*—should be revised in light of recent work demonstrating Bayesian multi-objective optimization for RHEA design (Islam et al., SSRN 7549378, Jan 2026), multi-fidelity active learning for TaNbMoVW (Jiang et al., J. Phys.: Mater. 9:025003, Feb 2026), closed-loop MPEA discovery (Priyadarshini et al., Mater. Horiz., Jul 2026), and LLNL's APEX autonomous DED platform (Mallia & Caputo, Aug 2026) (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000032).

**Suggested rewording:** *"While closed-loop Bayesian optimization and multi-fidelity surrogate strategies have recently been applied to alloy composition screening and individual AM process steps, no prior work has modeled the complete powder-to-elevated-temperature-property pipeline as a directed acyclic graph of heterogeneous surrogate nodes and optimized it via cost-aware Bayesian optimization of function networks with partial evaluations—where the algorithm autonomously decides when to query cheap nodes (CALPHAD simulations, single-track scans, density cubes, hardness maps) versus expensive terminal nodes (full elevated-temperature tensile/creep tests). This DAG-structured, partial-evaluation formulation applied to a physically executed, multi-stage additive manufacturing pipeline for refractory and superalloy systems is the core methodological novelty."*

This revision (i) acknowledges existing multi-fidelity and closed-loop work, (ii) specifies the DAG/BOFN/partial-evaluation architecture as the unique contribution, and (iii) ties the novelty to the physical AM pipeline rather than to computational-only optimization."}

## (a) Refractory Complex Concentrated Alloys and Nb-Based Alloys Processed by AM

**Brizes, E. et al., "A Dispersion-Strengthened Low-Density Niobium Alloy and Its Elevated Temperature Mechanical Performance," NASA Technical Report, Sep 2026. DOI: 10.64631/zcym1460**
Online: September 2026. NASA GRC/AFRL-relevant team fabricated an oxide-dispersion-strengthened low-density Nb alloy (LDNb-ODS) by LPBF from blended Nb521 + Ti64 + Cr + Y₂O₃ nanoparticle powder. ## Top 5 Things the PI Should Know

1. **The novelty claim needs tightening immediately.** At least three 2026 publications (Islam/Arroyave Bayesian multi-objective RHEA co-optimization; Jiang et al. multi-fidelity AL for TaNbMoVW; Priyadarshini et al. closed-loop MPEA discovery) use Bayesian or multi-fidelity optimization for complex alloy design. LLNL's APEX demonstrates a closed-loop DED-based alloy discovery platform. None, however, demonstrate cost-aware BOFN with partial evaluations across a physically executed multi-stage AM pipeline (powder → LPBF → microstructure → elevated-temperature property). The novelty claim must be narrowed to this specific DAG/partial-evaluation architecture.

2. **NASA's LDNb-ODS result (Brizes et al., Sep 2026) is the single most important refractory-AM benchmark.** It directly quantifies the performance gap the PI's platform should target: specific yield strength of 60–85 MPa/(g/cm³) to 800 °C, 10× improvement over C-103 in rupture at 1,093 °C, and oxidation as the life-limiting factor. This is from a NASA group (Smith, Kantzos) and should be cited in the one-pager.

3. **CALPHAD databases for refractory systems are expanding but remain incomplete.** Omprakash et al. generated DFT-informed pycalphad databases covering the full Cr-Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-V-W-Zr pool but lack liquidus/solidification data (omprakash2026firstprinciplesbasedpredictionof pages 8-11). Frey et al. emphasize missing interstitial (C, O) thermodynamics (frey2026aperspectiveon pages 28-30). These gaps directly support the PI's value proposition of coupling CALPHAD screening with experimental AM validation.

4. **GRX-810 yttria-content optimization (Chen et al., Jul 2026) narrows the design space for the secondary system.** The optimal window is 0.30–0.45 wt% Y₂O₃; above 0.5%, ductility degrades severely. This NASA co-authored result (with Gradl) is directly relevant to an AFOSR-aligned secondary demonstration (chen2026thecorrelationbetween pages 17-18, chen2026thecorrelationbetween pages 1-2).

5. **Elevated-temperature Al alloys for AM have advanced rapidly (Li et al., Nature Comms, Apr 2026).** A 582 MPa RT / 114 MPa at 400°C LPBF Al alloy with exceptional creep resistance at 400 °C sets a high benchmark for any bridge-system demonstration (li2026strongyetductile pages 1-6). The PI should frame the Al system as platform commissioning/validation, not an extreme-environment result per se.

---

## Suggested Wording Changes for the White Paper

The current claim—*"This cost-aware, partial-evaluation formulation applied for the first time to a complex additive manufacturing pipeline for alloys is the core methodological novelty"*—should be revised in light of recent work demonstrating Bayesian multi-objective optimization for RHEA design (Islam et al., SSRN 7549378, Jan 2026), multi-fidelity active learning for TaNbMoVW (Jiang et al., J. Phys.: Mater. 9:025003, Feb 2026), closed-loop MPEA discovery (Priyadarshini et al., Mater. Horiz., Jul 2026), and LLNL's APEX autonomous DED platform (Mallia & Caputo, Aug 2026) (mallia2026aiguidedselfdrivinglaboratories pages 12-17, mallia2026aiguidedselfdrivinglaboratories pages 6-12).

**Suggested rewording:** *"While closed-loop Bayesian optimization and multi-fidelity surrogate strategies have recently been applied to alloy composition screening and individual AM process steps, no prior work has modeled the complete powder-to-elevated-temperature-property pipeline as a directed acyclic graph of heterogeneous surrogate nodes and optimized it via cost-aware Bayesian optimization of function networks with partial evaluations—where the algorithm autonomously decides when to query cheap nodes (CALPHAD simulations, single-track scans, density cubes, hardness maps) versus expensive terminal nodes (full elevated-temperature tensile/creep tests). This DAG-structured, partial-evaluation formulation applied to a physically executed, multi-stage additive manufacturing pipeline for refractory and superalloy systems is the core methodological novelty."*

This revision (i) acknowledges existing multi-fidelity and closed-loop work, (ii) specifies the DAG/BOFN/partial-evaluation architecture as the unique contribution, and (iii) ties the novelty to the physical AM pipeline rather than to computational-only optimization.

**Brizes, E. et al., "A Dispersion-Strengthened Low-Density Niobium Alloy and Its Elevated Temperature Mechanical Performance," NASA Technical Report, Sep 2026. DOI: 10.64631/zcym1460**
Online: September 2026. NASA GRC/AFRL-relevant team fabricated an oxide-dispersion-strengthened low-density Nb alloy (LDNb-ODS) by LPBF from blended Nb521 + Ti64 + Cr + Y₂O₃ nanoparticle powder. Density was 6.73 g/cm³ with ~30 nm yttria dispersoids. Room-temperature UTS reached 1,005 MPa; specific yield strength of 60–85 MPa/(g/cm³) was maintained to 800 °C, surpassing Ni625, Ni230, and GRX-810 in that regime. At 1,093 °C/20.7 MPa, uncoated LDNb-ODS survived 21.4 h (10× legacy C-103), while R512E silicide coating extended life to 84.8 h. Oxidation—not creep—was the dominant life-limiting mechanism. Lack-of-fusion defects and Ti volatilization (31.5→24.8 wt%) were identified as processability challenges (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000003). **Tags: [CITE-1PAGER] [CITE-FULL] [COMPETITOR]** — This NASA result directly quantifies the performance gap the PI's platform should target and validates LPBF of Nb-based ODS alloys.

**Keller, T. et al., "Additive manufacturing of refractory niobium alloys: a review," Progress in Additive Manufacturing, 11:6491–6517, May 2026. DOI: 10.1007/s40964-026-01728-2**
Online: May 2026. Comprehensive review of AM Nb alloy processing covering LPBF and EB-PBF. Highlights that oxygen pickup can drive Nb ductility to nearly zero at ~1 at.% O, underscoring the importance of atmosphere control and powder handling throughout the pipeline (pqac-00000004). **Tags: [CITE-FULL]**

**Jabir, A.A.M. et al., "Investigation of process parameters to fabricate TiWMo refractory medium entropy alloy via LPBF," Progress in Additive Manufacturing, 11:5567–5577, Mar 2026. DOI: 10.1007/s40964-026-01648-1** *(earlier 2026)*
Online: March 2026. Elemental-blend LPBF of equimolar TiWMo produced a single BCC phase with 633 HV max hardness. Fine W powder (5–25 µm) at 350 W / 250 mm/s reduced unmelted W to 0.01%. Demonstrates a low-cost composition-screening route from elemental powders but does not report tensile ductility or elevated-temperature properties (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000038). **Tags: [CITE-FULL]**

**Rubio-Ejchel, D. et al., "Laser powder directed energy deposition fabrication and tensile sandwich evaluation of Ti64-C103-GRCop-42 functionally graded materials," J. Mater. Res., Sep 2026. DOI: 10.1557/s43578-026-01964-w**
Online: September 2026. CALPHAD/Scheil-informed LP-DED grading with C103 as intermediate bridge: Ti64→C103 gradient achieved >99% density and 390 MPa yield / 510 MPa UTS / ~45% local elongation in C103, but Cu–Hf intermetallics caused brittle failure at the C103→GRCop-42 interface (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000048, pqac-00000052). **Tags: [CITE-FULL]**

**Dodge, B.S. et al., "Ultrasonic atomization of a refractory high-entropy alloy TiZrNbHfTa for additive manufacturing," Powders, 5:25, Jul 2026. DOI: 10.3390/powders5030025** *(unobtainable — full-text verification needed)*
Directly relevant to the PI's rePOWDER ultrasonic atomizer: establishes ultrasonic atomization of a quinary refractory HEA. **Tags: [CITE-1PAGER] [CITE-FULL]**

**Xiao, B. et al., "Microstructure and mechanical properties of WMoTaNbV refractory high-entropy alloy via electron-beam powder-bed fusion," Appl. Mater. Today, 52:103378, Oct 2026. DOI: 10.1016/j.apmt.2026.103378** *(unobtainable)*
Timely EB-PBF data on the canonical W-Mo-Ta-Nb-V system. **Tags: [CITE-FULL]**

**Sowards, J.W. et al., "Solidification cracking of refractory alloys: a computational and machine learning study," Materials & Design, 263:115679, Mar 2026. DOI: 10.1016/j.matdes.2026.115679** *(earlier 2026, unobtainable)*
ML-based composition-dependent cracking prediction for refractory AM. Partially overlaps the proposed cheap-printability-surrogate node. **Tags: [CITE-1PAGER] [CITE-FULL] [NOVELTY-RISK] [COMPETITOR]** — The PI should position such models as constituent nodes within the DAG, not claim novelty of ML for refractory cracking prediction per se.

**Kumaravel, M. et al., "Mitigating the challenges in AM of refractory CCAs using Ti alloying via multi-material feedstock," MSEA, Jan 2026. DOI: 10.1016/j.msea.2026.149867** *(earlier 2026, unobtainable)*
Ti alloying as a ductilization strategy for RCCA LPBF. **Tags: [CITE-FULL]**

**Frey, C. et al., "A Perspective on the Historical and Contemporary Development of Refractory Alloys," Met. Mater. Trans. A, 57:461–503, 2026 issue. DOI: 10.1007/s11661-025-07996-x**
Identifies key gaps: minimum low-temperature ductility/toughness for crack-free printing is unknown; partition coefficients and solidus/liquidus data are sparse; current CALPHAD databases typically omit interstitial elements (C, O) despite their critical effects on cracking and ductility (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000026). **Tags: [AWARENESS]** — Treat as outside the primary window unless online-first date confirmed in 2026.

## (b) ML- or CALPHAD-Guided Design of RCCAs

**Ray, P. et al., "Electronic manifolds for extrapolative alloy discovery," Digital Discovery, Mar 2026. DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2603.06953** *(earlier 2026)*
Physics-informed pseudo-electron-density descriptors enable Bayesian active learning that predicts bulk modulus with <2% NMAE from only 10 training samples (~0.2% of dataset) in the Al-Nb-Ti-Zr space, and transfers zero-shot to the 7-component Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-V-W-Zr system; 20 actively selected target samples yield <3% NMAE (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000042). Demonstrates radical sample efficiency for RCCA property prediction. **Tags: [CITE-1PAGER] [CITE-FULL]**

**Peterson, N.E. et al., "Machine Learning Guided CALPHAD Design of Ru-Stabilized BCC B2 Refractory Alloys," arXiv:2609.14925, Sep 2026.**
Random-forest active learning coupled to Thermo-Calc TCHEA4 screened 500 compositions in the Nb-Ta-Mo-V-Ru-Ti-Zr-Hf-Al-Y space, identifying 100 meeting BCC+B2 stability, phase purity, and precipitate-fraction criteria at 1300 °C. Promising Nb-Mo-Ti-Ru-Hf-Zr and Nb-Ta-Ru-Hf compositions identified (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030). **Tags: [CITE-FULL] [COMPETITOR]**

**Omprakash, P. et al., "First-principles-based Prediction of Phase Fields: Part I. Binary and Ternary Refractory Alloys," arXiv:2609.06627, Sep 2026.**
DFT-informed pycalphad databases cover the full Cr-Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-V-W-Zr element pool, generating phase diagrams for 36 binaries through 126 quinaries. Liquidus data remain absent, making experimental solidification benchmarks valuable. This directly validates the PI's pycalphad pipeline and identifies where that pipeline adds value (pqac-00000025). **Tags: [CITE-FULL]**

**Shen, C. et al., "How Can Machine Learning Accelerate CALPHAD Free Energy Modeling?" arXiv:2606.01305, May 2026.**
Proposes ML surrogates for CALPHAD Gibbs energy functions spanning transition metals and refractory elements. **Tags: [AWARENESS]**

**Yan, Y. et al., "Machine learning-enabled discovery of refractory high entropy alloys on curated data," Research Square preprint, Aug 2026. DOI: 10.21203/rs.3.rs-10354540/v1**
Curated RHEA dataset with phase-label reassessment; F1=0.89 for predicting single-phase BCC stability, identifying mismatch in most-stable oxidation state (MSO_dv > 15) as a new ordering descriptor. **Tags: [CITE-FULL]**

**Islam, M.S. et al. / Arroyave group, "Bayesian multi-objective co-optimization of performance and manufacturability in BCC-B2 refractory high entropy alloys," SSRN 7549378, Jan 2026.** *(earlier 2026, unobtainable)*
**Tags: [NOVELTY-RISK] [COMPETITOR] [CITE-FULL]** — This work explicitly combines Bayesian multi-objective optimization with manufacturability constraints for RHEAs. It overlaps the PI's claim of "first" Bayesian optimization for AM RCCA pipelines. However, based on metadata, it appears to be a computational co-optimization rather than a physically executed AM loop with DAG-structured partial evaluations. The PI should sharpen the novelty claim accordingly.

**Jiang, T. et al., "Multi-fidelity, active-learning assisted design of TaNbMoVW refractory high-entropy alloys with superior mechanical properties," J. Phys.: Mater., 9:025003, Feb 2026. DOI: 10.1088/2515-7639/ae44d1** *(earlier 2026, unobtainable)*
**Tags: [NOVELTY-RISK] [COMPETITOR] [CITE-FULL]** — Multi-fidelity active learning applied specifically to TaNbMoVW RHEAs. This is the most direct semantic challenge to broad "first multi-fidelity optimization of RCCAs" language; however, it likely concerns computational fidelity layers (DFT vs. empirical), not the physical AM pipeline nodes with partial evaluations that the PI proposes.

## (c) Strategic-Element-Lean Superalloys for LPBF

**Chen, Y. et al., "The correlation between yttria content and thermal–mechanical properties of GRX-810," Progress in Additive Manufacturing, 11:8975–8992, Jul 2026. DOI: 10.1007/s40964-026-01834-1**
Online: July 2026. NASA co-authored (including Gradl). LPBF GRX-810 with 0.3–1.0 wt% Y₂O₃: the 0.30–0.45 wt% window gives the best strength–ductility balance. Above 0.5 wt%, as-built elongation drops from 27% to ~4%. HIP restores elongation to ~42% (≤0.45% Y₂O₃) or ~18% (>0.5% Y₂O₃) while reducing yield from ~785 to ~685 MPa. Thermal conductivity degradation from LPBF defects is also recovered by HIP. No new creep or oxidation data are reported in this paper (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009). **Tags: [CITE-1PAGER] [CITE-FULL]** — Sets a quantitative yttria-content target and confirms GRX-810 as a viable secondary demonstration system.

**Wassermann, N.A. et al., "Influence of melt pool overlap on inclusion entrapment and dispersoid characteristics in ODS Ni-20Cr fabricated by PBF-LB," SSRN 6635781, Jan 2026.** *(earlier 2026, unobtainable)*
Examines how melt-pool overlap during LPBF affects oxide-dispersoid trapping and distribution in Ni-20Cr ODS. **Tags: [CITE-FULL]**

**Ding, H. et al., "Dual-doped IN939 superalloy with superior strength and high temperature oxidation resistance via LPBF," MSEA, 961:150144, Jun 2026. DOI: 10.1016/j.msea.2026.150144** *(unobtainable)*
Dual-doped (likely Y₂O₃ + another species) IN939 by LPBF with enhanced strength and oxidation resistance. Relevant as an alternative strategic-element-lean superalloy approach. **Tags: [CITE-FULL]**

No ABD-900AM-specific paper or newly AI-designed Ni superalloy was found within the April–October 2026 window.

## (d) Elevated-Temperature Aluminum Alloys for AM

**Li, G. et al., "Strong yet ductile heat-resistant aluminum alloy by additive manufacturing," Nature Communications, 17, Apr 2026. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-71926-7**
Online: April 2026. LPBF produced an Al alloy with ~14 vol% heat-resistant multicomponent intermetallic nanophases (HMINPs) embedded in cell boundaries. Room-temperature UTS of 582 MPa; 114 MPa retained at 400 °C. Creep tests at 400 °C / 25–40 MPa demonstrated exceptional resistance. Partial solid-state amorphization of HMINPs at 300–400 °C provides an additional toughening mechanism (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000022). **Tags: [CITE-1PAGER] [CITE-FULL]** — This Nature Communications result raises the benchmark significantly for any Al-based bridge system, and the compositional details are worth checking for compatibility with the PI's atomization capability.

**Guo, D. et al., "Mechanical and in situ thermal-related behavior during DED AM of a high-performance Al alloy," Int. J. Extreme Manuf., 8:035002, Jan 2026. DOI: 10.1088/2631-7990/ae3349** *(earlier 2026)*
DED of an Al-Ni-Ce-Mn-Fe alloy using ultrasonic-atomized powder achieved <5 µm microstructure, <32 MPa residual stress, and 70%/50% improvements in yield/UTS over DED AlSi10Mg. Novel multimodal in situ characterization (synchrotron XRD + X-ray imaging + IR) elucidated phase evolution and stress accumulation during DED (pqac-00000023). **Tags: [CITE-FULL]** — Highly relevant to the PI's ultrasonic atomization → AM commissioning pathway.

**Bazaleeva, K.O. et al., "Deformation behavior of an Al-Ce-Fe-Ni-Zr alloy fabricated by L-PBF," Physical Mesomechanics, 29:931–943, Sep 2026. DOI: 10.1134/s1029959926600102** *(unobtainable)*
LPBF of an Al-Ce-Fe-Ni-Zr alloy — directly in the compositional space of interest for elevated-temperature Al alloys. **Tags: [CITE-FULL]**

## Novelty Risk and Competitor Assessment

**LLNL APEX** — The Autonomous Alloy Prediction and Experimentation platform is a DED-based self-driving laboratory integrating robotic handling, post-processing, and automated characterization (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033). It is classified as {MSS-3 (bulk metallurgy), HAL-2 (linked modules), SAL-2 (reactive closed-loop BO)}. Available evidence does not show it using BOFN, partial-evaluation fidelity management, or cost-aware node-selection decisions. **Tags: [COMPETITOR] [NOVELTY-RISK]** — APEX weakens generic "first autonomous AM alloy platform" claims but does not preempt the specific BOFN/partial-evaluation methodology.

**Priyadarshini, M.S. et al., "Machine learning-driven closed-loop discovery of hard multiple principal element alloys," Materials Horizons, Jul 2026. DOI: 10.1039/d6mh00103c** *(unobtainable)*
**Tags: [NOVELTY-RISK] [COMPETITOR]** — Closed-loop MPEA discovery. Blocks a blanket "first closed-loop complex-alloy discovery" claim.

**Zhao, L. et al., "Alloy design paradigms in additive manufacturing," Int. J. Extreme Manuf., 8:033003, Mar 2026. DOI: 10.1088/2631-7990/ae45de** *(earlier 2026)*
Proposes an "AI Auto-Lab for AM Materials" paradigm (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000034). Although primarily a roadmap, it makes generic "first autonomous AM alloy platform" language untenable. **Tags: [AWARENESS] [NOVELTY-RISK]**

---

## Top 5 Things the PI Should Know

1. **The novelty claim needs tightening immediately.** At least three 2026 publications (Islam/Arroyave Bayesian multi-objective RHEA co-optimization; Jiang et al. multi-fidelity AL for TaNbMoVW; Priyadarshini et al. closed-loop MPEA discovery) use Bayesian or multi-fidelity optimization for complex alloy design. LLNL's APEX demonstrates a closed-loop DED-based alloy discovery platform. None, however, demonstrate cost-aware BOFN with partial evaluations across a physically executed multi-stage AM pipeline (powder → LPBF → microstructure → elevated-temperature property). The novelty claim must be narrowed to this specific DAG/partial-evaluation architecture.

2. **NASA's LDNb-ODS result (Brizes et al., Sep 2026) is the single most important refractory-AM benchmark.** It directly quantifies the performance gap the PI's platform should target: specific yield strength of 60–85 MPa/(g/cm³) to 800 °C, 10× improvement over C-103 in rupture at 1,093 °C, and oxidation as the life-limiting factor. This is from a NASA group (Smith, Kantzos) and should be cited in the one-pager.

3. **CALPHAD databases for refractory systems are expanding but remain incomplete.** Omprakash et al. generated DFT-informed pycalphad databases covering the full Cr-Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-V-W-Zr pool but lack liquidus/solidification data (pqac-00000025). Frey et al. emphasize missing interstitial (C, O) thermodynamics (pqac-00000026). These gaps directly support the PI's value proposition of coupling CALPHAD screening with experimental AM validation.

4. **GRX-810 yttria-content optimization (Chen et al., Jul 2026) narrows the design space for the secondary system.** The optimal window is 0.30–0.45 wt% Y₂O₃; above 0.5%, ductility degrades severely. This NASA co-authored result (with Gradl) is directly relevant to an AFOSR-aligned secondary demonstration (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009).

5. **Elevated-temperature Al alloys for AM have advanced rapidly (Li et al., Nature Comms, Apr 2026).** A 582 MPa RT / 114 MPa at 400°C LPBF Al alloy with exceptional creep resistance at 400 °C sets a high benchmark for any bridge-system demonstration (pqac-00000017). The PI should frame the Al system as platform commissioning/validation, not an extreme-environment result per se.

---

## Suggested Wording Changes for the White Paper

The current claim—*"This cost-aware, partial-evaluation formulation applied for the first time to a complex additive manufacturing pipeline for alloys is the core methodological novelty"*—should be revised in light of recent work demonstrating Bayesian multi-objective optimization for RHEA design (Islam et al., SSRN 7549378, Jan 2026), multi-fidelity active learning for TaNbMoVW (Jiang et al., J. Phys.: Mater. 9:025003, Feb 2026), closed-loop MPEA discovery (Priyadarshini et al., Mater. Horiz., Jul 2026), and LLNL's APEX autonomous DED platform (Mallia & Caputo, Aug 2026) (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000032).

**Suggested rewording:** *"While closed-loop Bayesian optimization and multi-fidelity surrogate strategies have recently been applied to alloy composition screening and individual AM process steps, no prior work has modeled the complete powder-to-elevated-temperature-property pipeline as a directed acyclic graph of heterogeneous surrogate nodes and optimized it via cost-aware Bayesian optimization of function networks with partial evaluations—where the algorithm autonomously decides when to query cheap nodes (CALPHAD simulations, single-track scans, density cubes, hardness maps) versus expensive terminal nodes (full elevated-temperature tensile/creep tests). This DAG-structured, partial-evaluation formulation applied to a physically executed, multi-stage additive manufacturing pipeline for refractory and superalloy systems is the core methodological novelty."*

This revision (i) acknowledges existing multi-fidelity and closed-loop work, (ii) specifies the DAG/BOFN/partial-evaluation architecture as the unique contribution, and (iii) ties the novelty to the physical AM pipeline rather than to computational-only optimization.

contexts.context: The excerpt addresses refractory high-entropy alloy systems, particularly Nb–Mo–Ta–Ti–Zr and related modifications, in the context of LPBF. It states that refractory alloys are intended for high-temperature applications and generally crystallize in a BCC structure, unlike FCC Cantor alloys. Their high-temperature capability comes with reduced LPBF processability: they require higher volumetric energy densities (VEDs), and their low ductility makes them susceptible to thermally induced cracking. The excerpt identifies compositional modification as a principal strategy for improving printability and ductility. Substitution of zirconium with nickel suppressed crack formation and defects while retaining the BCC matrix and without severely narrowing the processing window. Other substitutions, including replacing Cr with Ti and adding Ta and B, produced a single-phase FCC alloy, indicating that phase engineering can alter the mechanical and processing response. The passage also mentions Cr3C2 reinforcement, which produced a refined columnar-to-equiaxed microstructure, an FCC grain-boundary network, and dispersed Cr3C2 precipitates. However, this excerpt does not provide specific DED or EB-PBF results, oxidation-resistance data, quantitative strength above 1200°C, or a detailed state-of-the-art assessment for hypersonic leading edges and thermal protection systems.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides detailed evidence for an additively manufactured refractory niobium alloy, LDNb-ODS, produced by laser powder-bed fusion (L-PBF) from blended Nb521, Ti64, elemental Cr, and nanoscale yttria powders. It reports substantial room- and intermediate-temperature strength: UTS is 1,005 MPa at 20 °C, 791 MPa at 550 °C, and 346 MPa at 800 °C. Strength decreases markedly at higher temperature, reaching a UTS of 29 MPa at 1,300 °C, although the alloy retains competitive specific yield strength through 1,100 °C and beyond 1,200 °C. Processing-related lack-of-fusion defects and microstructural inhomogeneity are identified as causes of inferior elevated-temperature performance relative to other low-density Nb alloys. Chemical segregation into Nb- and Ti-enriched regions promotes strain partitioning, thermally activated deformation, localized necking, and reduced ductility. At 1,093 °C, LDNb-ODS has better rapid-rupture resistance than Ni625 and C-103; oxidation, rather than creep alone, limits life. A fused-silicide R512E coating increases rupture life at 20.7 MPa from 21.4 to 84.8 hours. The excerpt does not provide comparative LPBF, DED, or EB-PBF data for Mo, Ta, W, Hf, Zr, Ti, or V, nor does it directly establish a broader state of the art for hypersonic leading edges or thermal-protection systems.

contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that process-parameter development for refractory-alloy additive manufacturing remains immature, although predictive processing maps—sometimes using approximate CALPHAD thermophysical data—can guide printing of several alloys. LPBF, DED, and EB-PBF are challenged by the widely different melting points of constituent elements: lower-melting elements may vaporize while higher-melting elements remain incompletely melted, producing chemical inhomogeneity, especially in blended-elemental powders. Ta- and W-containing alloys require higher energy input to obtain high relative density and suppress porosity. Printed refractory alloys can also exhibit an energy-density-dependent texture transition from <100> to <111>. Laser-parameter and scan-strategy changes alone have not prevented cracking in brittle Mo- and W-based alloys. Crack mitigation has included preheating at 800 °C or higher and environmental control, such as vacuum for EB-PBF or nitrogen for LPBF, but these measures must be combined with alloy-design approaches. Desired alloy characteristics include favorable solidification behavior, resistance to interstitial embrittlement, room-temperature ductility, and fracture toughness. Reactive carbides, rare-earth oxides, and reactive-element getter strategies can reduce cracking and refine grains. This excerpt does not provide quantitative elevated-temperature strength above 1200 °C, oxidation-resistance data, or a state-of-the-art assessment of hypersonic leading edges and thermal-protection systems.

contexts.context: This excerpt reports on a Ti-containing, yttria-dispersion-strengthened niobium alloy fabricated by laser powder-bed fusion (L-PBF), with vacuum heat treatment; it does not provide results for DED or EB-PBF, nor does it survey Mo, Ta, W, Hf, Zr, or V alloys broadly. A principal printability/compositional issue was substantial titanium loss: the printed alloy contained 24.8 wt% Ti versus 31.5 wt% in the calculated blend. Likely causes included oversized and low-density Ti64 particles being rejected by the recoater, displaced by shielding gas, entrained in the vapor plume, or evaporated. The material also exhibited elevated oxygen (0.124 wt%), far above the typical <0.03 wt% level for commercial Nb alloys, largely attributed to feedstock surface area and/or L-PBF processing. The resulting microstructure was very fine, with a 4.62 μm mean linear intercept, Ti-rich grain-boundary Ti(C,N) precipitates, and uniformly distributed ~31 nm yttria dispersoids. These features may improve creep resistance through boundary pinning and inhibition of dislocation motion. Tensile strength was up to 2.5 times that of C-103 through 600 °C, but C-103 surpassed it near 850 °C and above 1,000 °C. Nb alloys exhibit composition-sensitive cracking: strong Zr partitioning during solidification is associated with cracking, while Nb B-66 (Nb–5V–5Mo–1Zr) required a Mo + V/Zr ratio above 10.2 to mitigate susceptibility. The weldability table reports no defects for several Nb, Ta, and alloy grades, but solidification shrinkage in C129Y, combined solidification and solid-state cracking in D-43Y, and solid-state cracking in D-31. Mo and W are especially challenging; the excerpt suggests that avoiding cracking could permit useful ductility, and reports crack-free pure Mo with appreciable room-temperature tensile ductility under favorable texture. Proposed ductilization and printability strategies include minor ZrC or TiC additions to reduce DBTT and improve fracture toughness, environmental control, and grain refinement. contexts.context: The excerpt reports the latest findings for GRX-810, an oxide-dispersion-strengthened NiCoCr alloy produced by laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF), but it provides no results for ABD-900AM or other AI-designed nickel/cobalt superalloys. Yttria concentration strongly affects oxide-particle dispersion, agglomeration, defect formation, porosity, thermal conductivity, and tensile ductility, while its effect on thermal diffusivity is limited. The recommended composition window is 0.30–0.45 wt% Y2O3, which gives the most favorable strength–ductility balance. In the as-built/NHT condition, ultimate tensile strength is approximately 880 MPa for yttria contents below 0.45%. After hot isostatic pressing (HIP), compositions below 0.45% Y2O3 reach approximately 40% maximum elongation, whereas compositions above 0.5% show only about 18% elongation and approximately 825 MPa ultimate tensile strength. HIP lowers yield strength from roughly 785 to 685 MPa, attributed to grain coarsening, recrystallization, reduced dislocation density, and residual-stress relaxation, but improves ductility through pore closure, microcrack healing, and greater microstructural homogeneity. HIP also increases thermal conductivity at 900 °C by about 1.45 W m−1 K−1 (5.5%). No creep-life, creep-rate, rupture, or oxidation-performance data are included in this excerpt; the authors identify further microstructural work as ongoing.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies a recent Nature Communications study (Li et al., April 2026) on a strong, ductile, heat-resistant aluminum alloy produced by additive manufacturing, apparently using powder-bed fusion (PBF/LPBF). The reported characterization includes engineering stress–strain curves in both transverse and longitudinal directions from room temperature to 400 °C, comparisons of ultimate tensile strength versus temperature against other additively manufactured and conventional aluminum alloys, and tensile-creep curves at 400 °C under stresses of 25–40 MPa. However, the excerpt does not provide the numerical tensile-strength, elongation, or creep-rate/lifetime values, nor does it explicitly identify the alloy’s composition as Al-Ce, Al-Ni-Ce-Mn, or Al-Zr-Sc-Er. Microstructural evidence shows fine cellular structures, segregation of Al, Si, Fe, Mn, and Ni at cell boundaries, and multicomponent high-melting nanoprecipitates (HMINPs). After tensile testing at 400 °C, partial amorphization around nanoprecipitates and formation of a nano-dual-phase glass-crystal structure were observed. The authors interpret this partial solid-state amorphization as an additional high-temperature toughening mechanism. In-situ TEM indicates that deformation still involves dislocation accumulation, multiplication, crack initiation, and propagation. This is directly relevant as a recent LPBF heat-resistant alloy study, but the provided pages do not supply enough numerical data or coverage of DED and the specified alloy families for a full comparison.

contexts.context: This excerpt documents the experimental mechanical-testing framework for the 2026 Nature Communications study, “Strong yet ductile heat-resistant aluminum alloy by additive manufacturing.” The work concerns as-printed additively manufactured aluminum samples and evaluates tensile behavior at room temperature and elevated temperatures of 100, 200, 300, and 400 °C, using ASTM E8 and E21 procedures. Round specimens were machined from printed cylinders by EDM, with tests performed in both transverse and longitudinal orientations. Elevated-temperature tests used an initial strain rate of 0.005 min−1, increased to 0.05 min−1 at 0.8% strain; yield strength was calculated using the 0.2% offset method, and each condition was tested three times. Creep testing was performed on longitudinal specimens after heating to 400 °C and holding for one hour. The reported creep stresses were 25, 30, 32, and 40 MPa. The excerpt does not provide the alloy composition, whether the material is specifically an Al-Ce, Al-Ni-Ce-Mn, or Al-Zr-Sc-Er system, nor any numerical tensile-strength, yield-strength, elongation, or creep-life results. It therefore supports comparison of test temperatures, specimen orientations, strain rates, repeatability, and creep-loading conditions, but not the requested property values or a broader literature survey.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports a new laser powder bed fusion (LPBF/PBF-LB) approach for producing a heat-resistant aluminum alloy intended to address service temperatures of 300–400 °C. The strategy embeds heat-resistant multicomponent intermetallic nanophases (HMINPs) along solidification-cell boundaries, producing thermally stable cellular structures with approximately 14 vol% HMINPs. Without post-treatment, the as-printed alloy reportedly achieves an average room-temperature tensile strength of 582 MPa. At 400 °C, it retains a tensile strength of 114 MPa and exhibits exceptional creep resistance. During tensile deformation at 300–400 °C, partial solid-state amorphization of the HMINPs forms a nano-dual-phase glass–crystal structure, described as an additional toughening mechanism. The introduction contrasts this approach with conventional A201 and 2618 alloys, whose strengthening precipitates coarsen or have insufficient thermal stability, and with Al3Sc/Al3Zr systems, which have difficulty attaining high precipitate volume fractions. However, the provided pages do not identify the alloy’s full elemental composition and do not provide specific results for Al-Ce, Al-Ni-Ce-Mn, or Al-Zr-Sc-Er LPBF/DED systems. No directed-energy-deposition (DED) data are reported in this excerpt.

The alloy developed a refined microstructure, including eutectic colonies smaller than 5 µm and ultrafine eutectic lamellae. contexts.context: This excerpt reports a 2026 study of a bespoke Al–Ni–Ce–Mn–Fe alloy manufactured by directed energy deposition (DED), using ultrasonic-atomized powder. The alloy was designed for low cracking susceptibility and high thermal stability under rapid-solidification AM conditions. The paper’s main methodological contribution is multimodal in situ characterization combining synchrotron X-ray imaging, X-ray diffraction, and infrared imaging to quantify phase evolution, temperature distribution, thermal profiles, and stress accumulation during DED. The provided pages do not report creep testing, tensile results specifically at 300–400°C, or comparisons with additively manufactured Al–Ce or Al–Zr–Sc–Er systems. Thus, this source is relevant as evidence for a DED Al–Ni–Ce-containing alloy and its as-built strength and thermal-stability rationale, but it cannot establish elevated-temperature service performance from the supplied excerpt.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a first-principles-informed CALPHAD workflow for refractory alloys rather than a machine-learning-guided design framework. PyCalphad performs multiphase, multicomponent Gibbs-energy minimization using thermodynamic database (.TDB) files generated by a Python script. The databases include binary interaction parameters for BCC and HCP solid solutions, formation energies of stable binary intermetallics from DFT, elemental data from SGTE, and selected Materials Project intermetallic energies. The assessed element pool comprises Cr, Hf, Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, V, W, and Zr, directly covering refractory systems built from combinations such as Mo-Nb-Ta-W-Hf-Zr-Ti. All 36 BCC binary pairs were fit with sub-regular models; 21 HCP pairs involving Ti, Hf, and Zr were also fit, while 15 mechanically inappropriate HCP pairs used regular-solution models. The work generated composition–temperature diagrams for 36 binary, 84 ternary, 126 quaternary, and 126 quinary systems, although liquidus curves were omitted because high-throughput first-principles liquid modeling remains difficult. DFT calculations with VASP/PBE provide formation and mixing energies, while constrained calculations address mechanically unstable lattices. Phonon-based vibrational free energies were additionally used for the temperature-dependent ZrV2 C15 Laves phase. The excerpt does not report ML models or a dedicated database specifically named for the seven-element Mo-Nb-Ta-W-Hf-Zr-Ti system.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports that TiWMo refractory medium-entropy alloy was successfully fabricated by laser powder bed fusion with substantial in-situ mixing and rapid solidification. EDS indicated a largely uniform Ti and Mo distribution and an overall ternary mixture, although localized W-rich regions and partially dissolved tungsten particles remained; complete chemical homogeneity was not claimed within SEM–EDS limits. The main printability challenge was therefore melting and diffusing tungsten uniformly, particularly where coarse W particles or insufficient energy input produced unmelted material. Processing conditions were examined through P1–P3 powder blends and L1–L4 laser conditions. The results suggest that finer powder blending—especially smaller tungsten particles in P3—and increased energy density under L2/L3 improved melting, reduced unmelted W, and increased hardness. The alloy exhibited a dominant BCC solid-solution structure, with indexed (110), (200), and (211) reflections and a calculated lattice parameter of 3.21 Å. Its formation was supported by favorable calculated parameters: atomic size difference of 2.85%, VEC of 5.28, and mixing enthalpy of −4.356 kJ/mol. Microhardness was process-dependent; P1L1 and P1L4 had relatively low values of 548 and 549 HV, while refined blends and higher energy densities produced higher hardness through solid-solution and related strengthening mechanisms.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports successful fabrication of an equimolar TiWMo refractory medium entropy alloy using powder bed fusion laser beam (PBF-LB/M), with defect-minimized and compositionally uniform material obtained through optimized powder preparation and laser parameters. Printability challenges included coarse tungsten particles, insufficient energy input, unmelted W particles, reduced powder flowability and laser absorption, and lack-of-fusion defects. Tungsten pre-processing through extended dual-stage mixing with steel and silica balls, together with smaller W particles of 5–25 microns, improved powder handling, absorption, melt-pool homogeneity, and elemental uniformity. The best reported processing condition used 350 W laser power and a 250 mm/s scan speed; higher energy input and finer powder blends, especially P3, improved densification and mixing. The P3L2 condition produced the highest measured Vickers microhardness, 633 HV, followed by P2L2 at 623 HV and P3L1 at 618 HV. XRD indicated a dominant BCC solid-solution phase, while EDS mapping and line scans showed consistent Ti, W, and Mo distribution through the build. Hardness improvements were attributed to refined cellular/solidification structures, rapid solidification, solid-solution strengthening, more uniform composition, and Hall–Petch grain-boundary strengthening. The reported material is considered relevant to cutting and drilling tools, nuclear structural components, and aerospace thermal protection systems.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports that TiWMo refractory medium-entropy alloy could be fabricated by laser powder bed fusion using different powder blends, tungsten particle sizes, laser powers, and scanning speeds. Reducing tungsten particle size from spherical 45 µm powder to irregular 5–25 µm powder improved melting behavior and reduced residual unmelted tungsten. The P3L2 condition—5–25 µm W, 350 W laser power, and 250 mm/s scanning speed—had the lowest unmelted-W content among the examined samples. Across the tested conditions, the minimum measured unmelted tungsten fraction was 0.01% at an energy density of 280 J/mm³. Higher energy input generally improved melt-pool stability, wetting, inter-track and interlayer fusion, and densification, whereas lower energy input produced more pores and unmelted regions that could impair mechanical performance. Printability challenges included tungsten’s high melting point and limited dissolution time, which allowed some W particles to remain embedded, as well as powder-density differences among Ti, Mo, and W that could promote segregation. Powder pretreatment, 18-hour V-shaped mixing, and ball milling improved flowability and distribution. EDS indicated slight Ti enrichment near the titanium substrate, followed by gradual compositional homogenization; Ti, W, and Mo ratios largely matched the nominal composition along the build height, although complete homogeneity remained difficult.

contexts.context: Ray et al. describe a transferable electronic-manifold framework for extrapolative discovery in refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The method represents alloys using a pseudo-electron-density descriptor based on the superposition of atomic charges, rather than the fully converged DFT density. PCA shows that this descriptor recovers the trapezoidal geometry of the four-element composition/structure space and that four- and seven-component alloy datasets occupy overlapping manifolds. This suggests that local electronic packing environments, rather than explicit elemental identities alone, support transfer to elements absent from training. The approach removes the self-consistent-field (SCF) bottleneck from descriptor generation and is combined with Gaussian-process regression and Bayesian active learning. A model trained on 200 samples from the four-component Al-Nb-Ti-Zr domain demonstrated zero-shot predictive power for five-, six-, and seven-component alloys containing unseen Mo, Ta, V, and W. Few-shot adaptation using only 20 actively selected target-domain samples achieved NMAEs of 5.54% (R²=0.85) for five-component alloys, 4.16% for six-component alloys, and 2.87% (R²=0.68) for seven-component alloys. For in-domain bulk-modulus screening, fewer than 2% NMAE was achieved with 10 actively selected samples, indicating substantial sample and computational efficiency.

contexts.context: Ray et al. describe an electronic-manifold framework for extrapolative discovery in refractory BCC high-entropy alloys. Each alloy is represented by a pseudo-electron-density field constructed on a globally uniform absolute spatial grid, and spatial autocorrelations are reduced using principal component analysis. The first three PCs encode chemically meaningful structure—BCC periodicity, elemental density contrast, and compositional disorder—while higher PCs primarily represent stochastic noise. The approach deliberately uses unrelaxed pseudo-densities, avoiding expensive self-consistent electronic calculations and relaxation-induced volume and strain artifacts; this produces a smoother manifold suitable for composition-averaged properties such as bulk modulus and formation enthalpy. Transferability from D4 to D7 refractory-metal families is attributed to similar d-electron radial density profiles. Properties are learned with Gaussian Process Regression using an ARD squared-exponential kernel, which provides both predictions and uncertainty. Bayesian active learning then selects structures by maximizing predictive uncertainty relative to predicted property magnitude, reducing the number of ground-truth calculations needed. The excerpt reports an in-domain R² of at least 0.98 for the chemically relevant components. It does not provide a numerical speedup, total calculation reduction, or out-of-domain accuracy in the supplied passage. The method is not intended for configuration-sensitive properties involving local order, segregation, magnetism, defects, or finite-temperature sampling.

contexts.context: Ray et al. describe an electronic-manifold approach for extrapolative discovery in refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The method constructs spatial autocorrelation descriptors from unrelaxed, superposed pseudo-valence-electron densities generated from elemental pseudopotentials, avoiding the self-consistent-field (SCF) calculations needed to obtain converged charge densities. These descriptors encode chemically meaningful electronic structure and place related refractory transition metals in a continuously connected feature space, enabling regression across compositions rather than interpolation among disconnected clusters. A Gaussian process regression (GPR) model predicts composition-averaged properties, while active learning uses predictive uncertainty to select candidates for expensive DFT labeling. Training on the lower-order Al–Nb–Ti–Zr domain (D4) and testing without retraining on the refractory D7 domain (Mo–Nb–Ta–Ti–V–W–Zr) provides a zero-shot extrapolation test. For bulk modulus, active learning reaches normalized mean absolute error (NMAE) below 2% with only 10 total training samples (four random seeds plus six active acquisitions), compared with roughly 26 samples for converged-density descriptors and much larger datasets for typical methods. Even random sampling achieves R² = 0.98 and MAE = 1.41 GPa on D4, indicating strong global correlation and substantially reduced feature-generation cost.

contexts.context: Ray et al. describe an electronic-manifold representation for extrapolative discovery in refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The method represents each alloy using a pseudo-density field formed by a single-shot superposition of isolated-atom valence electron densities, avoiding the iterative self-consistent-field (SCF) procedure required for converged DFT charge densities. Two-point spatial autocorrelations of these fields provide high-dimensional descriptors, which are compressed with principal component analysis (PCA). The resulting low-dimensional electronic manifold is property-agnostic and captures composition-dependent spatial packing and valence-electron overlap; PCA produces a smooth composition geometry in which pure elements lie at vertices and alloys occupy the interior. Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) with Bayesian active learning is then used for prediction and efficient sampling. Reported performance for D4 is R² > 0.97 for both bulk modulus and formation energy, with bulk-modulus NMAE below 2%. contexts.context: Ray et al. describe an electronic-manifold approach for extrapolative discovery in refractory BCC high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The method builds a pseudo-electron-density descriptor by superposing isolated atomic valence densities in HEA special quasirandom structures (SQS), avoiding a self-consistent-field calculation. Two-point spatial autocorrelations are evaluated efficiently with FFT and reduced to three principal components, which are supplied to a Gaussian process regression (GPR) model. Bayesian active learning then selects candidates with the largest uncertainty or relative uncertainty for expensive DFT labeling, minimizing the number of calculations. For the D4 refractory alloy space, bulk modulus prediction reaches R² = 0.98 and 1.55% NMAE using only 10 actively selected samples; alloy formation energy reaches R² = 0.99 and 2.20% NMAE using 18 samples, with 88.8% and 99.8% uncertainty coverage within ±1σ and ±2σ. The descriptor transfers across both properties without modification and supports extrapolation to the chemically related D7 refractory BCC family after 20 selected D7 samples, although uncertainty becomes overconfident outside the training space. The claimed transfer is therefore intra-family, not arbitrary-chemistry extrapolation.
